Local review text and grid history are requested explicitly to keep ordinary reads small.

| Tool | Answers | Data access |
|---|---|---|
| `projects_list`, `project_overview` | Which projects exist; a compact overview with search totals, rank check and counts | Projects |
| `seo_report` | The weekly or monthly report as data: search totals against the previous period, top pages and queries, rankings, GA4, audits and top opportunities | Projects (each section also needs its own access) |
| `project_monitoring` | Alerts, report schedule, IndexNow setup and submissions (`kind`: alerts, reports, indexnow, budget) | Projects |
| `annotations_list` | The SEO change timeline: recorded website changes by date | Projects |
| `guide_list`, `guide_search`, `guide_read` | This guide | Projects |
| `search_performance_summary` | Clicks, impressions, CTR and position with the change against the previous period | Search |
| `search_queries_list`, `search_pages_list` | Top queries and pages, Google and Bing | Search |
| `forecasts` | 7, 14 or 28-day forecasts of stored daily series, scored earlier forecasts and the event calendar | Search |
| `keywords_list`, `keyword_research` | Tracked keywords with metrics; saved keyword research (ranked, gap, ideas) | Keywords |
| `rankings_summary`, `keyword_history` | Positions, visibility, winners and losers, and one keyword's history | Rankings |
| `serp_changes` | What changed on tracked results pages: features, competitors, new URLs, your movement, page types | Rankings |
| `ai_visibility` | AI Overviews, ChatGPT/Google AI mentions, brand-name matches and the Gemini/Perplexity answer checks | Rankings |
| `local_rankings` | Google Maps positions, ranking grids and the Business Profile | Rankings |
| `competitors_list`, `competitor_compare`, `backlinks` | Competitor visibility, gaps, who is ahead, and backlink profiles | Competitors |
| `opportunities_list`, `seo_tasks_list` | Opportunities with evidence and action plans; assigned work and due dates | Opportunities |
| `site_audit`, `browser_audit` | The latest crawl with issues and affected pages; saved browser and Lighthouse diagnostics | Opportunities |
| `pages_list`, `page_details` | Known URLs and everything stored about one URL | Pages |
| `analytics_summary` | GA4 organic sessions, conversions and revenue | Pages |
| `web_vitals` | Core Web Vitals field data per checked URL, with weekly history | Pages |
| `page_changes` | Watched pages and detected title, description, H1, canonical, noindex and status changes | Pages |
| `seo_change_impact`, `indexing_status` | Before/after comparison around a recorded change; saved Google indexing evidence | Pages |
| `content_briefs_list`, `content_brief_details` | Saved writing plans and their original evidence | Pages |

The three search tools combine Google and Bing by default. Ask for one engine with `source`: *google* or *bing* (for example "Bing clicks of the last 28 days"). Combined figures use Google's average position, because Bing reports none per day. Page details read stored data without fetching another paid lookup.

Before drawing conclusions, the assistant can call `data_quality` (Projects): it lists which datasets are current, stale, sampled or missing, so a missing import is never read as zero.

Before starting new research, it can read `investigations_list` and `investigation_get` (Keywords) to reuse what was already found, and call `research_on_file` (Keywords): the lookups and analyses the project already has, with market, inputs, date and whether they are still current. Opportunities come with a `score_breakdown` (demand, relevance, impact, confidence, effort, risk, evidence and the priority formula), the same one the opportunity page shows.

## Changes an assistant may make

Only with the matching box ticked on the token (or on the sign-in page):

| Tool | Does | Permission |
|---|---|---|
| `annotation_create`, `annotation_update` | Adds or edits a note on the SEO change timeline | Change notes |
| `seo_task_save` | Creates or updates the team task of an opportunity | Team tasks |
| `content_brief_create`, `content_brief_update` | Creates a brief (prefilled from stored data) or edits one | Content briefs |
| `opportunity_set_status` | Done, dismissed, open again, or snoozed until a date | Opportunity status |
| `page_watch_set` | Starts or stops weekly checks for up to 50 URLs | Page watches |
| `keyword_set_relevance` | Marks up to 50 keywords relevant or not relevant for the business, or back to automatic | Keyword relevance |
| `cluster_set_owner` | Sets the page that should own a topic, or clears it | Topic owners |
| `investigation_save`, `investigation_add` | Starts or updates an investigation; adds dated sources, checks, limitations, notes or a finished analysis | Keep research notebooks |

Changes use the permissions of the user who created the token, so a viewer's token cannot change anything. Each change is logged and shows "via <token name>" on the note, brief or task. If someone changed the same record in the meantime, the assistant gets a conflict and has to read it again; it never overwrites. Ask the assistant for changes in plain words, for example "Record that we rewrote the shoe category titles today" or "Assign the duplicate-title task to Sam, due Friday".

Practical questions: "Give me last month's SEO report for Web Shop", "Which pages fail Core Web Vitals on mobile?", "What changed on our watched pages this week?", "What do Gemini and Perplexity answer for our prompts?", "Forecast clicks for the next 28 days", "Which opportunities have an action plan and who is working on them?".

## Safety

- Every call is **logged** in the audit log (tool, project, result), never with its content.
- A token acts **for the user who created it**. It stops working when that user loses access.
- Limit: 60 requests per minute per token.
- Treat a token like a password. If one leaks, revoke it and create a new one.

09.title: 9. Users, workspaces and security
09.text:
# 9. Users, workspaces and security

## Workspaces

A **workspace** holds projects, integrations (Google, DataForSEO), AI tokens and members. Agencies typically use one workspace per client team; everyone else needs only one. If you belong to several workspaces, switch between them at the top of the sidebar.


### Creating a workspace

The installation administrator creates workspaces: click **New workspace** below the workspace name at the top of the sidebar, enter a name and click **Create workspace**. You become its owner and switch to it right away; add members under *Workspace → Members*. If your licence allows no further workspace, the page says so.

### Renaming and deleting

*Workspace → Settings*:

- **Owners and admins** can rename the workspace.
- **Owners** can delete it. Type the workspace name to confirm. Members lose access immediately, and all projects of the workspace are deleted with it, including their scheduled imports and rank checks. The data stays in the database but is no longer shown anywhere.

A workspace cannot be deleted if it is the installation's only workspace, or if you have no other workspace to continue in.

## Roles

| Role | Can |
|---|---|
| **Owner** | Everything in the workspace, including deleting it |
| **Admin** | Everything except deleting the workspace: projects, integrations, members, AI tokens, audit log |
| **Member** | View and edit projects, start paid analyses (metrics, rank checks) and site audits |
| **Viewer** | View projects only |

Projects can additionally be limited to certain members. A foreign project is simply not found.

The **installation administrator** (created by the installer) also manages the installation itself under *System*: health, jobs, backups, updates and the Google app.

## Team members

*Workspace → Members* lists who has access to the workspace and with which role. Owners and admins also manage members there.

### Adding a member

Under **Add a member**, enter the person's e-mail address and choose a role (Admin, Member or Viewer).

- **The address already has an account** (for example a colleague in another workspace): the person is added right away.
- **New person:** you get an **invitation link**. Copy it and send it to them yourself, for example by e-mail or chat, because SEO Control Center does not send e-mails. On the link's page, they choose their name and password and can then sign in.

The link is shown **only once**, works once and expires after **7 days**. Open invitations are listed under *Open invitations*. If a link is lost or went to the wrong person, **revoke** it and add the person again.

### Changing roles and removing members

- Change a member's role in the table and click **Save**.
- **Remove** takes away the person's access to this workspace immediately. Their account remains, along with any other workspaces they belong to.

Some limits keep a workspace safe:

- the **Owner** role cannot be given here;
- only an owner can change or remove another owner;
- nobody can change their own role or remove themselves.

Every change is recorded in the **Audit log**.

## Your account

Click your name at the bottom of the sidebar to open **Your account**:

- **Name:** change it at any time.
- **E-mail address:** this is the address you sign in with. Changing it asks for your current password.
- **Password:** enter your current password and the new one twice. All your other sessions, for example on another computer, are signed out; the current one stays signed in.

After five wrong current passwords, these changes are locked for 15 minutes.

## Managing users (installation administrator)

**System → Users** lists every account of the installation with its workspaces, two-factor status and last sign-in. For each user you can:

| Action | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Deactivate** | The user can no longer sign in. Their sessions end immediately and their AI access tokens stop working. Nothing is deleted. |
| **Reactivate** | Undoes a deactivation. |
| **Reset two-factor** | For a lost phone: the user signs in with their password alone and can set up two-factor sign-in again. |
| **Send reset link** | E-mails the user a link to choose a new password (needs *System → E-mail*). |
| **Make admin / Remove admin** | Gives or takes the rights to manage the installation (*System*). |

You cannot deactivate yourself or remove your own administrator rights, and the last active administrator always stays. Every action is recorded in the audit log.

Workspace roles (owner, admin, member, viewer) are managed per workspace under *Workspace → Members*.

## White label (installation administrator)

**System → Branding** shows SEO Control Center under your own brand: in the app, on the sign-in page, on report pages and in report e-mails.

- **Product name:** replaces "SEO Control Center" in the sidebar, the browser tab and reports.
- **Accent colour:** a hex colour such as `#0f7b6c`. It is used for buttons, links and highlights in light and dark mode, and for the button in report e-mails.
- **Report footer:** replaces "Sent by SEO Control Center" at the end of reports, for example "Prepared by Your Agency · hello@your-agency.example".
- **Logo:** PNG, JPEG or WebP, up to 512 KB, shown 30 pixels high. Report e-mails show the name only, because e-mail programs do not load images.

The sender name of e-mails is set under *System → E-mail*. Empty fields keep the defaults.

## Forgot your password?

On the sign-in page, click **Forgot your password?** and enter your e-mail address. You receive a link to choose a new password; it works once and for 60 minutes. Afterwards all your sessions are signed out and you sign in with the new password.

This needs e-mail to be set up under *System → E-mail* ([chapter 2, step 7](02-installation.md)). Without it, the page tells you to ask your administrator.

When e-mail is set up, **invitations** are sent by e-mail too, and members who already had an account get a short note that they were added.

## Signing in securely

Under **Account security** (also linked from *Your account*):

- **Two-factor sign-in:** scan the QR code with an authenticator app and confirm with a code. Store the **recovery codes** somewhere safe; each one works once if you lose your phone.
- **Sessions:** *Sign out other sessions* ends every session except the current one, for example after using a shared computer.

Further protection:

- repeated wrong passwords are slowed down and limited;
- sessions end after a period of inactivity;
- every sensitive action is recorded in the **Audit log**.

## Your data

- All SEO data stays in **your own database** on your server.
- Passwords are stored only as secure hashes. Google and DataForSEO credentials, and two-factor secrets, are stored **encrypted**.
- SEO Control Center contacts only these services:
  - **Google**, for Search Console;
  - **DataForSEO**, if connected;

10.title: 10. Backups and updates
10.text:
# 10. Backups and updates

## Backups

**System → Backups → Create backup now** saves the whole database as a compressed file on your server. The newest 7 are kept. A backup needed to recover an unfinished update is protected from automatic cleanup until that update succeeds.

- **Download backups regularly**, or make sure your host's backup includes the folder `seo-control-center/storage/backups`, so a copy exists outside the server.
- **The encryption key is never in a backup.** Keep the offline copy of `storage/keys` from the installation ([chapter 2, step 6](02-installation.md)). Without it, stored passwords and tokens in a restored database cannot be decrypted.
- Every update creates a backup first.
- *System health* warns when the last backup is older than 7 days.

**Restoring** replaces the whole database. It is done on the command line (`php bin/console backup:restore <file> --force`). If you have no shell access, ask your host.

## Updates

Updates are signed packages (`scc-<version>.zip`). Your installation only accepts packages signed with the project's release key, and only if every file is intact.

1. Download the **update package** from the [project's releases](https://github.com/seoccnet/seo-control-center/releases). (The install package, `scc-<version>-install.zip`, is only for new installations.)
2. Go to **System → Updates**, choose the file and click **Upload and verify**. The page shows the version and what the package contains.
3. Click **Install**.

The update:

1. switches the site to maintenance mode;
2. creates a consistent database backup;
3. replaces the changed files and updates the database;
4. switches maintenance mode off.

This usually takes less than a minute. During the active installation request, all pages temporarily show a maintenance notice so they cannot load partially replaced application files. After that request finishes or stops, administrators can sign in and reach *System → Updates* to recover a failed update.

If a step fails after file replacement begins, the page says which one and the site stays in maintenance mode. Retry the same signed package: completed database migrations are skipped and interrupted migrations can resume. This also works when the installed version already shows the target release. The original database backup is kept under *System → Backups* and is reused for recovery; a retry does not replace it with a backup of the partially updated database. Keep the pending package until recovery succeeds.

Schema updates are forward-only. If retrying still fails, restore both the original database backup and the matching application files with your host. Restoring the database alone does not roll back the application files. Keep your offline encryption-key backup available.

SEOcc doesn't look for updates by itself. To hear about new versions, watch the repository's releases on GitHub.

11.title: 11. Troubleshooting
11.text:
# 11. Troubleshooting

## Where to look first

**System health** checks the installation and shows each problem with a hint:

- PHP and hosting;
- the database;
- storage;
- encryption;
- backups;
- cron;
- the job queue.

**System → Jobs** lists background jobs that failed, with the reason. After fixing the cause, click **Retry**, or **Dismiss** the job if it no longer matters.

## Common problems

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| Nothing updates: no imports, no rank checks | Cron is not running. *System health → Cron* shows when it last ran. Check the cron command and the PHP path ([chapter 2, step 5](02-installation.md)). |
| *Cron* warning although cron is set every 5 minutes | Add `CRON_INTERVAL_MINUTES=5` to `.env` |
| "Needs reconnection" for Google | Access was withdrawn at Google. Connect again under *Integrations*. If it happens every 7 days, your Google app is still in *Testing*; publish it ([chapter 5](05-google-search-console.md)). |
| DataForSEO "refused access" | Usually an unverified account or no credit at DataForSEO. Fix it there, then click *Test connection*. |
| Rank checks stop with a budget message | The daily or monthly budget is used up. Raise it under *Integrations → DataForSEO*, or wait for the next day or month. |
| "is turned off on this installation" | An administrator listed that feature in `DISABLED_FEATURES` in `.env`. Remove it to turn the feature on. Your data stays available meanwhile. |
| Update refused: "not a valid package" / "signature" | Use the original, unmodified update package (`scc-<version>.zip`, not the install package) from the project\'s GitHub releases |
| A page shows "Error 419" | The form expired, for example after a long pause. Reload the page and try again. |
| Site shows "being updated" for a long time | An update stopped midway. Sign in and open *System → Updates*: it shows the failed step. Install the same package again. |

## Two-factor sign-in

- **Lost your phone?** Sign in with one of your **recovery codes** instead of the app code.
- **No codes left?** Another administrator can help, or contact support.

## Support

Please include, in a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/seoccnet/seo-control-center/issues):

1. a **support bundle** (*System health → Download support bundle*). It contains health checks, versions and recent errors, with e-mail addresses and tokens removed, and never passwords, keys or SEO data;
2. what you did, what you expected, and what happened.

12.title: 12. Site audit
12.text:
# 12. Site audit

The site audit checks your website the way a search engine sees it. It follows the links between your pages and reports technical problems: broken links, redirects, missing titles and more.

## Running an audit

Open a project and go to **Site audit → Start audit**. The audit runs in the background with every cron run, and the page updates itself while it works. Depending on your server and the cron interval, about 500 pages take 10 to 30 minutes. You can leave the page; the results are there when you come back. **Stop** cancels a running audit.

Owners, admins and members can start audits; viewers can read the results.

## What is checked

| Severity | Issue |
|---|---|
| Error | Broken page (4xx), server error (5xx), page not reachable, missing title |
| Warning | Redirect chain, internal link over `http://`, duplicate title, missing or duplicate meta description, missing H1, response slower than 2 seconds, HTML larger than 2 MB |
| Notice | Not linked internally (in the sitemap, but no checked page links to it), redirect, title longer than 60 or shorter than 10 characters, meta description longer than 160 characters, several H1 headings, noindex, canonical pointing elsewhere, fewer than 200 words, blocked by robots.txt |

Four growth notices point at improvements rather than errors and do not lower the health score:
- **No structured data**: no JSON-LD or microdata. Product and article pages get a hint about the markup to add.
- **Article without an author**: no byline, author markup or author meta on an article page.
- **Article without source links**: an article of 600 words or more whose text links to no other site. Menus, cards, footers and your own pages do not count.
- **Structured data without the page's own type**: the page has structured data, but only for the site (breadcrumbs, organization). A product page, by its Open Graph type, has no Product markup, or an article has no Article markup.
- **Product or category page without answered questions**: a product page, or a category page marked as a collection or item list, with no heading phrased as a question (H2 to H4, or an accordion title) and no FAQ markup. Google no longer shows FAQ rich results; answering buyers' questions is still worth it for visitors and AI answers.
- **Product page without a specification table**: no table or list of terms (three entries or more) with the product's key facts.
- **Deep in the site structure**: more than three clicks from the start page.
- **Business details missing**: checked once per audit on the start page and any contact page (an address ending in contact, kontakt, impressum, imprint, about, o-nama and similar). It lists what neither states:
  - Organization or LocalBusiness structured data;
  - a phone number as a `tel:` link or in the markup;
  - an address in structured data.

  It is reported on the start page. Pages crawled before 0.46.0 did not record these details, so the check waits for the next audit.

These appear as opportunities with their own action plans.

Title, description, heading and text checks apply only to pages that are meant to be indexed. The pages of a paginated listing (`?page=2`, `?page=3`, …) usually share a title, so they count as one page for duplicate titles and descriptions. Pages with *noindex*, or with a canonical tag pointing to another address, are listed once as such and not checked further.

## Reading the results

- **Health score:** 100 means that no checked page has an error or a warning. Pages with an error count fully against the score, and pages with warnings only count half. The arrow shows the change since the previous audit.
- **Issues by type:** how many pages have each issue, and how that changed since the previous audit. Click a type to see its pages and advice on fixing it.
- **Linked from:** for broken pages, redirects and blocked pages, up to three pages that link to them, so you know where to fix the link.
- **All checked pages:** every address with its status, title, word count, links, response time and depth (clicks from the home page; "—" when no link from the home page leads there).
- **Export CSV:** all issues of the audit as a spreadsheet.
- **Long titles worth fixing first:** click *Title too long* to see which long titles cost clicks.
  - **By page type:** how many long titles each page type has (the first part of the address, such as `/tastes/…`), how many of them are on Google's first page, and the clicks they miss together. Many long titles of one type usually come from one template, so fixing the template fixes them all.
  - **Pages first:** up to 20 pages in positions 1–10 with at least 100 impressions in the last 28 days of Search Console data, ranked by the clicks they get below your site's usual rate at that position. The rate comes from your site's own clicks by position, or a general curve while your own data is thin. Each page shows its title as cut at 60 characters, about what fits in a result, so you see what searchers see.

  A shortfall can also come from the search itself, such as ads, an AI Overview or a brand search. The title is one likely reason, not proof. Pages with too little search data are counted but not ranked.

The last 5 audits are kept, so you can open an earlier one from the **Audits** list.

## Settings

Project editors can configure the free audit below. Browser checks are requested separately.

## Internal links

Open **Improve → Internal links**. It uses the newest completed free audit and your topics with an owner page (*Research → Topics & owners*).

- **Link suggestions** lists paragraphs on your pages that mention a topic word for word (one of its searches, plurals included) but don't link to the page that owns it from their text yet. A link in the menu, header, footer or sidebar doesn't count, because it doesn't replace a link in the text. Pages that compete for the topic get no suggestion for it. A search that has its own page (an address ending in that search, also when the search adds words, such as *regular tomato seeds* for /regular-seeds) is left to that page. Only sentences count: paginated copies of a page and short product lines are skipped. The section says when the suggestions were built. The matched words are highlighted: add the link there, or around similar wording that reads naturally. Topics with more demand, and pages that already get many internal links, come first. There are at most 5 suggestions per topic and 3 per source page. Filter by topic or page address.
- **Reword with AI** opens Ask AI with a prepared request to rewrite the paragraph around the link. It sends nothing until you press send.
- **Links of one page** shows, for an address the audit crawled, every link into and out of it. Each link shows its anchor text, where it sits (text, menu, header, footer, sidebar) and, for links in the text, the paragraph around it.

Suggestions are rebuilt within the hour after an audit completes and once a day, so a new owner page shows up without a new crawl. The crawler reads server HTML only: links that JavaScript adds are not seen. Paragraphs are kept only for the newest audit. No suggestion means your pages already link where they mention a topic, no topic has an owner page yet, or no paragraph uses a topic's searches word for word.

AI assistants can read the same data with the `internal_links` tool (*Pages* permission).

## Browser-rendered site audit and Lighthouse

Under **Site audit**, choose an HTTPS start URL already known under Pages on the current project domain. Choose a mobile browser crawl of 1, 10, 50 or 100 pages, or a one-page Lighthouse mobile diagnostic. Browser estimate: $0.0051 per selected page limit; Lighthouse estimate: $0.005 per task. Existing API budgets apply. This is separate from the free weekly HTML crawl.

Cron checks robots/public DNS, submits the page, then retrieves the saved task in later runs. Same-page retries retrieve unfinished saved tasks without buying them again. Unknown submission outcomes block replacement checks until usage is reviewed. Previous completed evidence stays visible while a check is pending or fails.

For a failed known task, **Retry saved check** retrieves it again for free. **Start new paid check** explicitly buys a replacement, useful when old provider results have expired. Neither action overrides an uncertain submission outcome.

Results show rendered title/description/headings, sampled links, loaded resource entries and declared CSS/image references, provider findings and lab LCP/CLS. Lab numbers describe one browser run; Google CrUX separately reports real-user p75 LCP/INP/CLS. The browser check does not provide INP or an overall field-data pass/fail assessment, and does not change the free crawl's health score.

DOM samples are capped at 100 links, 20 H1s and 100 resource references. CSS backgrounds come from the first 100 DOM elements and image sources from the first 40 images. Provider resource statuses are retrieved in resumable batches, capped at 10,000 resource rows and 6 MB per crawl; each waterfall lists up to 1,000 resources. Provider-loaded CSS resources are included. Popup dismissal can be requested, but is not proof of consent. General scroll/click/consent journeys and complete unloaded CSS traversal are not supported; resources appearing later may be absent. Declared references are not proof that those resources loaded.

The latest five completed browser/Lighthouse diagnostics can be reopened. Browser metadata and proven 404/410 resource findings feed Opportunities and printable/email reports as separate browser findings. Lighthouse shows category scores, navigation metrics and up to 50 diagnostics; total blocking time is not INP, and lab scores are not a field-data pass.

New browser checks also retain a separate **Lazy-image candidates** sample: up to 40 declared URLs from `data-src`, `data-original` and `data-lazy-src` on the first 40 images. Placeholder sources do not hide these declarations, and a full loaded-resource sample does not crowd them out. Candidates are deduplicated and resolved against the page URL; they are not fetched or labelled as successful loads or broken assets. Empty samples mean no matching declarations in that sample. Older snapshots show this evidence as unavailable. Responsive declarations have their own sample; scrolling and interaction-only content remain outside these samples.

**Responsive-image candidates** lists up to 40 distinct URL declarations from `srcset` and `data-srcset` on the first 20 images and `<picture>` sources combined. At most 20 attributes are retained, each no longer than 2,048 characters; longer attributes are omitted rather than truncated. URL tokens retain embedded commas; unsupported schemes such as data URLs are filtered out. The sample does not validate descriptors, evaluate media conditions or format support, or predict which image the browser selects. These declarations are separate from loaded resources and do not create broken-resource findings. Older snapshots show responsive evidence as unavailable.

New snapshots record the browser's document base URL under **Reference base URL**. Relative declarations resolve against it, including when an HTML `<base>` points to a CDN; absolute references keep their own address. The audited page's identity and crawl scope remain unchanged. An invalid or unsupported supplied base leaves relative references unavailable while valid absolute references remain. Older provider responses without base evidence use the audited page URL. References remain passive evidence and trigger no extra fetches.

CSS background sampling also inspects `::before` and `::after` on the first 100 DOM elements. Resource evidence marks these as `css_before_background` and `css_after_background`. Loaded entries and ordinary element backgrounds are sampled first; all resource references share the existing 100-reference cap, so a full sample can omit later declarations. Each background value is sampled up to 16,384 characters. These references do not establish visibility, HTTP status or successful loading, and do not create broken-resource findings by themselves. This is computed-style sampling, not exhaustive stylesheet traversal.

Free sitemap startup now persists its pending documents and robots cache between cron runs. Each startup step makes at most one HTTP request. Robots redirects follow up to five guarded public HTTPS hops, persisting each hop before continuation; redirects alone never grant crawl permission. HTTP reserves do not provide a hard deadline guarantee for host operating-system DNS resolution.

## Free audit settings

Project editors can set:

- **Pages per audit:** 100, 250, 500 (default), 1,000 or 2,000. The audit stops when it has found this many addresses.
- **Audit the site every week:** a new audit starts automatically 7 days after the last one.

## How the crawler behaves

- It starts with your home page and the pages in your sitemap (the sitemap listed in robots.txt, otherwise `/sitemap.xml`). Sitemap pages fill at most 80 % of the page limit, so pages that are only linked stay included.
- It follows paginated listings up to page 10; products further back are usually in the sitemap.
- Page discovery stays on your project's domain, with and without `www.`, over HTTPS. A separate bounded resource pass can check referenced assets and external-link destinations; it does not crawl those websites.
- It identifies itself as `SEO-Control-Center` and follows your robots.txt: the rules for `SEO-Control-Center`, otherwise the rules for `*`. To exclude parts of your site, add for example:

  ```
  User-agent: SEO-Control-Center
  Disallow: /shop/cart
  ```

- It loads one page at a time, so it does not put your server under load.
- It does not log in, submit forms or run JavaScript. Resource checks read at most 1 KB to establish reachability; they do not render images or execute scripts. Pages that only show their content after JavaScript runs may be reported as having little text.

## Referenced assets and external links

For each HTML page, SEOcc samples up to 15 image/script/stylesheet references and five external links, with at most 500 distinct targets per audit. It follows each target host's robots rules, requires public HTTPS destinations and does not follow redirects.

- Missing image `alt` attributes are notices. An explicitly empty `alt` is valid for a decorative image.
- HTTP asset URLs are mixed-content warnings; HTTP targets are not fetched.
- A 404 or 410 is a broken-asset or broken-external-link warning.
- Transport failures and server errors are resource-unavailable notices. A 403, 429, redirect or robots exclusion is not labelled a proven broken link.

Issue details list sampled URLs on the referring page. Checks are bounded samples, not a complete browser rendering: CSS background images, dynamically injected resources and lazy-loading attributes are outside this pass. The page-crawl count can reach its limit while resource checks are still finishing. Stopping the audit also stops remaining resource checks.

If the audit reports that your domain *does not resolve to a public address*, the domain points to a private network address and cannot be checked from your server.

13.title: 13. AI assistant and spending
13.text:
# 13. AI assistant and spending

## Ask AI

The **Ask AI** button at the bottom right of every page opens a chat with Claude or GPT, whichever your workspace chose. It reads your stored SEO data and answers in your language, for example:

- "What should I work on first this week?"
- "Why did my traffic drop in September?"
- "Which sites should I ask for a backlink?"
- "How visible am I in ChatGPT compared with my competitors?"

The assistant knows which project you are looking at. While it reads data, the chat shows what it looked at (for example *Read: SEO opportunities*). It is instructed to use stored evidence and explain missing data. Check important numbers against the underlying section, especially when a result is incomplete or sampled.

### Prompt library

When the chat is empty, it shows ready prompts in eight categories: Performance, CTR & snippets, Queries & intent, Pages & content, Countries & devices, Rankings & competitors, Technical & indexing, and Plan & report. During a conversation, **Prompts** in the chat header opens the same library. Selecting a prompt puts it in the message box, so you can change the dates, thresholds or URL first. Press Enter to send.

The prompts are written for the data SEOcc stores, for example:

- "Show me queries with at least 500 impressions and a CTR below 1 % in the last 28 days, sorted by impressions."
- "Show me queries containing "how to", "what is", "why", "which" or "can"…"
- "What was my CTR in the United States last week compared with the week before?"

Questions like these use filters that search every stored Search Console query and page, not only the top rows: text the query or URL contains, minimum impressions, CTR and position ranges, word count, new or lost queries, and the biggest gains or losses against the previous period. Country and device figures are totals for the whole site. Search Console data in SEOcc has no country breakdown per page or query, and the assistant says so when asked.

### Tables, charts and downloads

Answers can contain tables, lists and charts. Each answer has **Copy** (the text as Markdown) and **Download .md**. Tables have **Copy table**, which pastes into Sheets or Excel, and **Download CSV**. Charts have **Copy data** and **Download SVG**. Charts are drawn only from numbers the tools returned. **Export** in the header downloads the whole conversation as a Markdown file. The arrow button next to it makes the panel wider for tables and charts.

It can **mark opportunities** as done, dismissed or open again, but only after you click **Confirm** in the chat. If you write something else instead, nothing changes. It starts no paid lookups.

### Fixing issues with Ask AI

Every opportunity has an **Ask AI** button. It opens the chat and asks for the cause and the exact changes for that item. For technical issues, the assistant reads the affected pages from the latest site audit, with their current title, description, status and redirect target. It answers with concrete changes per page, for example "/trail-shoes: change the title from *Shoes* to *Trail Shoes – Acme Shop*".

When the changes cover several pages, the chat shows a **Download fix plan** link. The CSV lists each URL with the issue, the current value and the suggested change, ready to hand to whoever edits the website. The assistant cannot change your website itself.

When the changes are made, tell it "I fixed it, check again". It proposes a new **site audit**; click **Confirm** to start it. Audits are free and take a few minutes. The opportunities then close by themselves once the problems are gone.

Your conversation stays when you move to another page. **New chat** starts over. Each person's conversations are private.

### Waiting, retries and efficient questions

When the provider is busy or rate-limited, Ask AI shows a waiting period and enables **Try again** afterwards. It never retries automatically. Chat and optional digest summaries share the same workspace/provider cooldown. Repeated failure of the same step is limited to three attempts per hour.

If a browser request times out or loses its connection, use **Refresh conversation** first: the server may already have completed it. Refresh reads saved messages without another model call. An incomplete provider answer is labelled and stops; ask a narrower follow-up to continue. Concurrent requests for your conversation are rejected while one is running.

Use one focused question with a project, date range and URL or keyword. The model sees the last three question turns within a 90 KB limit; **New chat** helps when changing topics. Each question has at most eight model steps and each response at most six tool calls. Duplicate reads are suppressed and large results are explicitly bounded. These controls reduce unnecessary work; they cannot guarantee a fixed token cost or perfect answers.

Budgets are checked before a call. Known rejected calls release their reservation. If a provider connection fails after sending the request, SEOcc keeps the estimated charge conservatively because the provider may have processed it. An explicit retry may cost again. Local spending totals can differ from the provider invoice.

### Setting it up

1. Create a key:
   - **Claude:** in the [Claude Console](https://console.anthropic.com/settings/keys);
   - **GPT:** on the [OpenAI platform](https://platform.openai.com/api-keys).

   Add credit under *Billing* first.
2. Go to **Integrations → AI assistant**, choose a model and paste the matching key. The model decides the provider:
   - **Claude:** Sonnet 5.5 (balanced), Opus 5.5 (most capable) or Haiku 4.5 (fastest, cheapest);
   - **GPT:** GPT-6.1 Sol (balanced), GPT-6 Astra (most capable) or GPT-6 Luna (fastest, cheapest).
3. Set daily and monthly **budgets**. A question usually takes one to four calls; with Sonnet or Sol, a call costs about $0.01–0.05. When a budget is reached, the chat says so.

Owners and admins can set up the assistant; every member of the workspace can use it.

## DataForSEO spending

The top bar shows what DataForSEO cost this month and what to expect by the end of the month, for example **$8.29 → $40.47**. The small bar fills up towards the monthly budget and turns amber or red when the forecast gets close to a limit or passes it.

Click it for the details:

- today and this month;
- the forecast and last month;
- the budgets and what is left;
- your DataForSEO balance and how many days it lasts at the current pace;
- a 14-day chart;
- the spending per feature.

The forecast adds the average of the last 14 days for each day left in the month.

It is shown to members who can start paid lookups. Owners and admins change the budgets under **Integrations → DataForSEO**.

14.text:
# Pages and insights

Page details also shows [saved Google indexing evidence](23-google-indexing.md): reported coverage, last crawl and canonical, with its check time and any latest failure. **Inspect or watch this URL** opens Google indexing. Viewing a page makes no inspection request.

Page details also show recorded changes for the exact URL and site-wide notes within the displayed period. Use [SEO change annotations](19-seo-change-annotations.md) to record edits and review their context without assuming they caused subsequent results.

Open **Project → Pages** to list the URLs SEOcc knows from connected search data, rankings, the latest completed crawl, stored backlinks and GA4. This is a catalog of stored URLs; it is not a guarantee that every URL on your website has been discovered.

## Content inventory

**Research → Content inventory** lists every page, draft and planned article SEOcc knows about. There is one row per address, with what each source says about it, and each source keeps its own status and date:
- the latest site audit crawl, with redirects, canonicals, noindex and errors;
- the sitemap watched by IndexNow;
- Search Console impressions;
- content briefs and articles marked as published from ideas;
- topic-plan pages and topic owners;
- your CMS records.

A CMS draft is not a public page, a canonical is not a redirect, and a page without rankings still exists. The *Sources* box says how far each source reaches and when it was last read.

SEOcc has no CMS connection. Add drafts and scheduled posts by hand (**Add a CMS record**), or paste a CSV export under **Import a CMS export**:
- `title` and `status` columns are required; `url`, `publish_date`, `cms_id` and `note` are optional;
- WordPress statuses (publish, future, draft, pending, private, trash) are understood;
- a row with a known `cms_id` updates that record instead of adding a second one.

Addresses are matched without tracking parameters (`utm_…`, `gclid`), a trailing slash or the http/https difference. Other query parameters, and www against non-www, are kept apart.

A record without an address may be a page that already exists. SEOcc shows it as a *Possible match* but never joins it on its own; choose **This is the page** to confirm. Edits use the record's version, so two people cannot overwrite each other.

**Before new content.** Article ideas and new content briefs check the inventory. When an article page, a draft, a scheduled post, a brief or an article published from an idea already covers an idea's main search, the idea shows *Already in your content inventory*, so you improve or publish that instead of writing a duplicate. Shop, category and other pages on the topic are listed as *Other pages on this topic, not articles*: they exist, but they do not answer an informational search. Link them to the new article. Pages kept in a topic plan or owning a topic are not taken to cover that plan's subject; they only link to it.

### Overlap review

From the inventory, **Overlap review** lists pages and plans that may cover the same thing:
- **Near-duplicate text**: two pages whose body text is mostly the same. Text repeated on many pages, such as delivery notes, is left out, and so are listing pages: paginated copies (`?page=2`), author archives, and tag, topic and category archives, which have their own check.
- **Several pages for one search**: from Topics & owners. This is often fine, for example a category and a guide; it mainly hurts when the leading page keeps switching.
- **Article ideas on the same subject**: two ideas worded differently, such as "mold on pepper" and "pepper mold".
- **Topic archives splitting a subject**: two archives on one subject: the narrower archive's words are all in the other, or the two share most of their distinctive words. Words used in many of your archive addresses (for example "outdoor tomato" on a growing blog) don't count. Archives that differ only in such words come first. When one archive adds words of its own ("yield" and "high yield indoor pepper"), the pair comes later and is marked as a possible subtopic, because a parent and a child archive can both be useful.

At most 100 candidates of each kind are listed, strongest first; the counts include them all. Each candidate shows its evidence and what is uncertain. When the pages are of different kinds (a shop page and an article) or serve different purposes, it says they may need to stay separate. The page-kind check knows common shop and article addresses; a shop that keeps products under its own folder, such as `/seeds/`, may not get that note.

**Before a merge: what each page is and gets** shows each page's state, 28-day clicks and impressions, any redirect or canonical, and the topics it owns. It also proposes the address to keep: the target of another page's redirect or canonical first, otherwise the page with the most clicks.

Choose **Decide** to record *Keep separate*, *Merge planned* (with the page to keep) or *Undecided*, with a note. Nothing is merged automatically and SEOcc changes nothing on your site: carry out a planned merge in your CMS and add a change note.

## Everything about one URL

Open a URL to see its Google and Bing clicks, Google search queries, tracked rankings, latest audit issues, AI Overview citations, open opportunities and sampled backlinks. When connected, GA4 adds Organic Search sessions, key events and purchase revenue, and CrUX adds mobile Core Web Vitals.

Google query rows omit some anonymized searches, so they do not always add up to page totals. Search clicks and GA4 sessions are different measurements. Missing data means the source has not supplied it, rather than a zero result.

## What to improve

Each URL detail view starts with a ranked summary of useful next actions. SEOcc places audit errors before significant Google click declines, then ranking gains, audit warnings, internal links, possible overlapping intent, matched open opportunities and audit notices. This order is a review heuristic, not a prediction of ranking impact. Each candidate shows up to three supporting examples, a suggested next action and a link to the full evidence below.

Click declines compare the displayed 28-day search window with the preceding 28 days. Both periods need a completed Google page import for every day and stored metrics for the exact URL. A decline candidate requires at least 100 previous clicks and a drop of 30% or more. Missing metrics are not interpreted as zero; Bing weekly buckets are not compared.

Ranking candidates use Google queries at average positions 4–20 with at least 50 impressions, or stored tracked keywords at positions 4–20. Review the source dates and search intent. No candidates means only that the available evidence did not meet these rules; it does not establish that the page is problem-free.

When the page could gain many clicks, *Improve rankings within reach* moves up. With about 200 or more extra clicks it comes right after audit errors, ahead of click declines. With 50 or more it stays just behind click declines. Its first line says how many clicks are at stake.

## What the page could gain

Three sections under the search queries show what the page could gain and what was already tried:

- **Worth reaching the top 3:** for each search at positions 4–20 with at least 50 impressions in the window, the clicks now, the clicks expected at position 3 and the difference, at most five searches with the largest difference first. The expected clicks come from your site's own clicks by position across its non-brand searches, blended with a general curve where your own data is thin. It is an estimate: AI Overviews, ads, maps and the intent of the search all change how many people click.
- **Pages ranking above it:** when a *Why they outrank you* analysis from the last 180 days included this page, the page is compared with the readable pages ranking above it in that analysis, up to five. Each measure (words, questions answered, tables, lists, images, videos, structured data types, internal links) shows this page's count against the median of the pages above. A measure below 60 % of that median is marked *Behind*, and *What to improve* adds *Close the gap with the pages above it*. Counts describe the pages, not why they rank: add what helps searchers, never filler to match a number. To see this for another page, run the analysis on a keyword topic the page ranks for.
- **Changes to this page and their results:** up to ten changes recorded on this exact URL in the last year, newest first, with the measured metric, the result and its effect, read the same way as on *Manage → Change timeline → What worked*. A change without a plan shows *No measurement plan*; open it to add one.

The summary uses stored data and does not start imports, paid lookups or AI calls. Ask AI and MCP `page_details` receive the same recommendations and comparison availability. Their existing permissions remain unchanged.

## Possible cannibalization

The Pages view highlights queries where several pages compete in the top 20. It requires at least 200 query impressions, and each candidate needs at least 50 impressions and a 10% share. Review the intent and the pages before deciding to consolidate or rewrite content; several ranking pages are not always a problem. A notice appears when the analysis reaches its row limit.

## Internal link suggestions

SEOcc uses the latest completed crawl's link graph and relevant titles or H1s to suggest indexable, self-canonical pages with incoming links that could link to a page ranking at positions 4–20. Existing links are excluded. Suggestions do not edit your website; review and add useful links yourself.

### Kinds of links

Each internal link found by the site audit is classed:
- *In the text*: a link inside a sentence of real text;
- *Related-article card*: a card linking to another article;
- *Product or cross-sell card*;
- *Menu, footer or sidebar*: template links, breadcrumbs included;
- *Other body link*.

Each class shows a confidence (high, medium, low): page regions and class names are clear signals, while a heading or image card is a weaker one. For one page, **Links of one page** groups the links by class. A footer or menu link that repeats on every page counts once, with the number of pages that carry it. For an audit crawled before 0.35.0, links in the page body show as *Not classified* until the next site audit.

Only a link *in the text* stops a suggestion: a related-article card or a menu link to a page leaves room for a link in the paragraph. Before suggesting a link, SEOcc also checks that the paragraph and the target are about the same kind of thing. "Free seeds" in a paragraph about earning reward points is not suggested as a link to a prize-draw page; the left-out matches are counted. The box **What the link evidence covers** gives the crawl size and date and the limits the suggestions are built under. No suggestion for a page does not prove it is well linked.

## Ask about the page

Ask AI can read the page's stored evidence. Connected MCP clients can use `pages_list` and `page_details` when their access includes **Pages** (`pages:read`). Existing tokens do not gain this permission automatically; create a token or approve a connection with the scope you need.

## Backlinks by page

From **Backlinks**, request live links or links lost in the last 30 days. Each result stores up to 1,000 links and is a sample, not a complete count. Page details reuse the stored samples without another provider charge.

Weekly lost-link monitoring is paid and off by default. Review its estimated cost and your DataForSEO budgets before enabling it. It also refreshes lost referring domains so stored strong-link losses can feed alerts.

15.title: Analytics and Core Web Vitals
15.text:
# Analytics and Core Web Vitals

Connect Google Analytics 4 to understand Organic Search landing-page results, and Google CrUX for real mobile and desktop field performance. Both are optional and need their own Google setup.

**Integrations → Connection guides** includes illustrated GA4 and CrUX setup steps, original Google screenshots and links to the relevant console screens. The same guides appear on each provider’s settings page. Google’s Analytics demo is a reporting example; Google does not allow its demo properties to be imported through the Data API.

## Connect Google Analytics 4

Enable the **Google Analytics Data API** in a Google Cloud project. Create a service account and grant its e-mail address **Viewer** access to your GA4 property. Under **Integrations → Google Analytics 4**, an owner or administrator supplies the service account's JSON credential. SEOcc encrypts it and does not display it again. This connection is separate from Search Console.

Under **Project → Analytics**, link the numeric GA4 property ID and start an import. Daily imports can then keep the latest 28 completed days current. Changing the linked property clears the previous property's imported data. Disconnecting the workspace credential stops imports while retaining stored results.

If an import fails, check **System → Jobs**. Errors distinguish service-account authentication from the GA4 report request, and recognized Google reasons identify disabled APIs, permission or policy refusals, invalid authentication and quota exhaustion. Check that the credential saved in SEOcc belongs to the service account granted access to the selected property. Saving credentials or linking an ID does not prove Google access; a successful import does. Unknown responses show a generic error without exposing private Google response content.

## Understand the analytics figures

Imports include **Organic Search** sessions, **conversions (GA4 key events)** and **purchase revenue** for the project's bare and www hostnames. Conversions may be fractional because of attribution. Purchase revenue uses the property's currency and can include negative adjustments.

Dates use the property's timezone. Results show privacy thresholds and row-limit notices: an import is capped at 10,000 daily rows. Reports with missing imported dates display a partial-period warning. These figures also appear in page details and reports. Search clicks and sessions should not be expected to match.

## Import history and compare periods

Daily imports refresh the latest 28 completed days while retaining earlier imported dates. Under **Project → Analytics**, select 28, 90, 180 or 365 days before requesting an import. Larger imports consume more Google quota and may exceed the 10,000-row cap; a limited import is visibly marked.

Use the start and end date filters for a period of up to 365 days. Each landing page can show changes in sessions, conversions and purchase revenue against the immediately preceding period of the same length. Both periods need imported coverage for every date, including successful dates with no rows. Missing dates are unavailable rather than zero; comparisons are suppressed when either compared period contains limited or privacy-thresholded imported dates.

Only history matching the currently reported property currency and timezone is included. Older rows with a different currency/timezone remain stored but are not added together. Changing the linked property explicitly clears its previous history. Page details use their displayed reporting dates rather than lifetime imported totals.

## Business measurement

Sessions alone do not say whether search brings business. Under **Project → Analytics → Business measurement**, name the GA4 events that count as success for this project:
- a purchase (`purchase`);
- a qualified lead (`generate_lead`);
- a subscription or sign-up (`sign_up`);
- another goal, by its exact GA4 event name.

Find the exact names in GA4 under Admin → Events; case matters. A project can have up to ten business events.

Each event shows one of five states:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Not configured | No business event is defined, so SEOcc cannot tell whether organic visits lead to results. |
| Unknown | GA4 is not connected or linked, or not every day of the period is imported. A missing count is not zero. |
| Import failed | The last GA4 event import failed. The error is shown; the landing-page import is not affected. |
| Not observed | GA4 recorded none over fully imported days. Nothing may have happened, or the tag, consent banner or event name may not be set up. Treat business value as unverified, not zero. |
| Observed | GA4 recorded the event, shown site-wide and in Organic Search sessions. |

The period ends on the last imported GA4 day. The section also shows GA4 Organic Search sessions next to Search Console clicks for the same dates. Search Console runs two to three days behind, so its count is often marked *Partial* with the days it covers. They measure different things (sessions include Bing, need the tag and consent, and restart after 30 minutes), so they never match one to one. The limits list covers consent, time zones, currency, attribution, privacy thresholds and what SEOcc cannot see: it reads GA4 reports only and cannot check whether your site's tag fires on a page.

**Check a test conversion.** Make one conversion yourself on your live site (a test order, a test lead form or a test sign-up), then choose **Check GA4 now** within 30 minutes. At the next cron run SEOcc reads GA4's realtime report, read-only, and shows which business events GA4 received. A count above zero shows that GA4 received the event, not which page or channel sent it. SEOcc never buys, submits or sends anything itself.

When GA4 records no key events or revenue, opportunity value estimates say "unknown" instead of zero.

The Quest Log's *Connect Google Analytics* quest has two more steps: name your business events, then see GA4 record one of them. If you finished the quest before these steps existed, it shows as in progress again until they are done.

## Connect Core Web Vitals

CrUX field data and optional paid browser/Lighthouse Site audit checks are separate. CrUX reports mobile or desktop real-user p75 LCP, INP and CLS with rolling collection dates. Browser diagnostics report lab runs and do not provide INP or an overall field-data pass. Missing metrics remain unavailable; SEOcc never substitutes origin data for a page. Invalid device/URL records and collection dates are rejected.

Enable the **Chrome UX Report API** in Google Cloud. Under **Integrations → Core Web Vitals**, supply an API key restricted to that API. From a known URL in **Pages**, an editor can request a field-data check. Google quotas apply.

SEOcc sends requests from the hosting server. If you restrict the key by application, use the server's outbound IP addresses; website/referrer restrictions block server requests. A shared hosting address may differ from the outbound address. System → Jobs shows recognized Google rejection reasons for IP/referrer/API restrictions, disabled APIs and invalid keys. A 403 means access was refused; it does not indicate missing field-data coverage.

Page details show separate mobile and desktop 75th-percentile **LCP**, **INP** and **CLS**, with their rolling collection dates. Editors can enable weekly refresh for up to 50 page/device watches per project. Cron checks up to 50 due watches each hour; a configured Google API key is required. The latest 52 snapshots per URL/device are retained. SEOcc requests URL-level data and does not silently substitute an origin-wide result. A low-traffic URL may have no data; that is not a pass or fail.

## Speed tests (lab)

Open **Improve → Speed tests**. A profile saves a test setup, so its runs can be compared with each other: one page, mobile or desktop, and a source.

- **PageSpeed Insights** is free. It uses the Google API key saved under **Integrations → Core Web Vitals**. Enable the **PageSpeed Insights API** in Google Cloud and, if the key has API restrictions, allow it for the key too. A new PageSpeed profile runs once right away.
- **DataForSEO Lighthouse** is paid (about $0.005 per run, from the workspace budget). Tick the confirmation each time you start a run.

Each run shows Lighthouse's performance score (0–100), LCP, CLS, TBT, FCP and Speed Index. The latest 8 runs are listed, with the score change since the previous run. Switch on **Repeat weekly** to test automatically once a week. Up to 10 profiles per project; the newest 50 runs of each profile are kept.

Lab runs simulate a page load under fixed conditions; they are not what visitors experience. Each profile therefore shows the field data of the same page and device beside its runs (if fetched under Pages), and the two are never mixed. Compare runs within one profile, not across sources or devices. TBT stands in for INP, which only exists in field data.

### Why a run scored as it did

Open **Why the latest run scored N** under a profile. It is read from the report Lighthouse returned for that run, so it costs nothing extra:

- **Largest Contentful Paint element**: what the LCP was (for example the hero image), its markup, the image address, and how the time split: TTFB, load delay, load time and render delay. The phases come from the page load Lighthouse observed, before its simulated throttling, so they don't add up to the run's LCP; read them as shares, and start with the largest. On Lighthouse 13 (PageSpeed Insights since late 2026) it also lists the request discovery checks: whether the image has `fetchpriority=high`, can be found in the HTML, and is not lazy-loaded.
- **Render-blocking resources**: style sheets and scripts that hold back the first paint, with how long and how large.
- **Top diagnostics**: audits below a good score, largest estimated saving first. The savings are Lighthouse's estimates for this run, not a promise, and they do not add up. Items without a saving or value (for example *Network dependency tree*) follow as *Also flagged*.
- **Requests by type** and the **largest requests**.
- **Test configuration**: device and screen, throttling (round trip, bandwidth, CPU slowdown), Lighthouse version and the test machine's benchmark, the tested address and user agent. PageSpeed Insights does not report its throttling or screen: it uses fixed mobile or desktop settings, so its runs are compared by Lighthouse version only.
- **Raw report**: its SHA-256, size and fetch time, plus the DataForSEO task for paid runs. SEOcc does not keep the full report.

Runs saved before 0.38.0 have only their metrics; the next run adds the diagnostics.

### Comparable runs

PageSpeed Insights updates Lighthouse from time to time, and a new major version scores differently. A run tested with another Lighthouse major version, throttling or screen size than the run before is marked **Different setup**. The profile then says why instead of showing a score change. Compare its later runs with each other.

AI assistants can read profiles, runs and field data with the `lab_tests` tool (*Pages* permission), including the latest run's diagnostics and whether each run is comparable with the one before.

## Where the results appear

Field data appears in **Pages** and **Site audit**, separately from crawler response timing. Opportunities can flag results with a collection window ending within the last 35 days when LCP exceeds 2.5 seconds, INP exceeds 200 milliseconds or CLS exceeds 0.1.

These are field measurements from real Chrome visits, not a Lighthouse laboratory test or a speed score generated by SEOcc.

16.title: Local branches and reviews
16.text:
# Local branches and reviews

Use **Local → Locations and review texts** for a business with several branches. Each additional branch has its own Google Maps identity, search area, language, keywords and check history.

## Add a branch

An editor supplies a label, exact numeric Google Maps **CID**, coordinates, language and keywords. SEOcc matches that CID rather than treating every branch on a shared website as the same business.

Run a point check manually or opt into weekly checks. Paid checks use your workspace's DataForSEO account and budget; the estimate is shown before you enable the schedule. Branch point checks cover one configured area.

## Compare a branch across its neighbourhood

Expand **Branch visibility grids** in the branch card. Select one of its keywords, a 3×3, 5×5 or 7×7 grid, and point spacing from 250 to 5,000 metres. Each grid is centred on that branch's saved coordinates. The screen shows estimated costs for each size; requesting a grid requires permission to run paid analyses and an available budget.

Cron checks one missing point at a time and saves progress before continuing. The heatmap matches the branch's exact CID, so another store sharing its website cannot count as this branch. A missing position means it was not found within the checked depth. Only one grid per branch runs at a time, and the latest 12 grids are shown. Weekly branch checks remain point checks; they do not automatically buy grids.

If a grid fails, inspect **System → Jobs** and usage before requesting another one. Completed points remain visible. Branch identity and search area remain fixed for consistent history.

## Keep the history consistent

You can edit a label or keywords and stop weekly checks without deleting history. A branch's CID, area and language are fixed for its history; create another branch for a different identity or search area. Removing a branch deletes its stored history.

## Import review texts

Request a review sample manually for a configured branch, or for the primary location once its CID has been discovered. The paid import requests up to **100 newest reviews**, including original text when available, author, rating, timestamp and owner reply.

The provider prepares the task asynchronously. SEOcc polls the saved task without another paid submission, for up to 24 hours. Weekly position checks do not fetch review texts automatically.

If a submission fails ambiguously, check **System → Jobs** and usage before manually requesting another import. SEOcc does not automatically repeat a potentially paid submission. A missing review in a sample does not prove it was deleted.

The reviews imported for the primary location feed **Review handling** on the Local page and the finding *Answer your Google reviews*. Import them again after a few weeks to see whether the reply share and the pace of new reviews have changed.

17.title: Alerts and weekly digest
17.text:
# Alerts and weekly digest

Under **Your account → Notifications**, choose the alerts and digest you want, mute individual projects and review alerts from the last 30 days. Your installation needs configured e-mail delivery under **System → E-mail**.

## What triggers an alert

SEOcc checks stored data hourly for keywords leaving the top 10, weekly clicks falling by at least 30% from a baseline of at least 100 clicks, new site-audit errors, lost strong backlinks and low DataForSEO budget or balance.

After a rank check, it reports **results-page changes** that matter: an AI Overview appearing for a keyword where you rank in the top 10, you leaving the top 10, or a tracked competitor entering the top 10 above you. See *Research → Results-page changes* for all changes.

It also reports changes in Google's indexing verdict or selected canonical after two successful [URL inspections](23-google-indexing.md). Initial results and failed checks do not create change alerts. Google returns its stored index evidence; a change is a reason to investigate, not a confirmed technical cause. The indexing/canonical alert type can be muted like other project alerts.

Alerts do not start paid lookups. They depend on current imported data, completed audits and stored backlink results. Each event is sent once. You receive project alerts only for projects you can see; budget alerts require integration-management permission.

## Your Monday digest

The weekly digest brings together the latest complete week's clicks, top-10 keywords, site health, winners and losers, opportunities, alerts and a report link. It covers up to ten visible projects per workspace and is sent on Mondays in UTC.

An AI summary is optional and off by default. It uses the workspace's configured assistant and counts against its AI budget. Without a working assistant or sufficient budget, the digest goes out without that summary.

## Control what you receive

Turn off individual alert types, mute a project's notifications or disable the digest in your account settings. Alerts stay available in Notifications even when e-mail delivery is not configured; enabling mail later does not send an old backlog.

## Tune project alert sensitivity

Project editors can expand a project under **Project alert sensitivity** and choose:

- Traffic drop: 1–100%, default 30%.
- Minimum clicks in the previous seven days: 1–1,000,000, default 100.
- Ranking cutoff: top 1–100, default top 10. An alert means a keyword left this group between checks.
- Minimum lost-link domain rank: 0–100, default 30. Unknown domain ranks are excluded.

These settings apply to all recipients of the project, starting with the next hourly scan. Existing alerts and their once-per-event history remain intact. Audit-error and budget rules are unchanged.

## Send project alerts to your team

With integration-management permission, open **Team alert delivery** for a project.

1. For Slack, create an incoming webhook in your Slack app settings and select its channel. Choose **Slack incoming webhook** in SEOcc and paste that URL.
2. For another service, choose **JSON endpoint** and paste a public HTTPS URL accepting POST requests. Optionally supply a bearer token. SEOcc does not follow redirects or connect to private network addresses.
3. Enable delivery and save. The next new project alert is sent by cron. **Recent delivery attempts** shows whether the endpoint accepted it. Past alerts are not replayed.

The generic JSON payload contains `event` (`scc.alert`), `id`, `type`, `title`, `lines`, `url` and `created_at` (UTC). The `X-SCC-Event-ID` header repeats the event ID for receiver-side deduplication. Use authentication on your endpoint and keep webhook URLs secret.

URLs and tokens are encrypted and are never redisplayed. Leave them blank to keep them; clear the token or remove the destination to revoke it. Saving changes invalidates deliveries already queued for the old configuration.

Team delivery is independent of personal email mutes. It covers project alerts, not workspace budget alerts or weekly digests. SEOcc rechecks the configuring user's current permission before sending. Each event has one delivery attempt: after an interrupted or uncertain transfer, check the receiving service before taking action. Automatic retries could send duplicates. Live Slack or endpoint setup requires your own verification.

18.title: Using the interface
18.text:
# Using the interface

The refreshed interface is available from version 0.9.36. Subsequent polish described here becomes available when that update is installed.

## Finding a project tool

The workspace menu contains Dashboard, the Quest Log ([chapter 26](26-quest-log.md)), Projects, Integrations and workspace administration. System administrators also see the installation's system tools. On a phone or narrow tablet, use **Open navigation** in the top bar. Close it with the same button, by clicking outside it or with Escape.

Project tools are grouped by purpose:

| Group | Tools |
|---|---|
| Traffic | Overview, Performance, Analytics |
| Research | Pages, Keywords, Rankings, Competitors |
| Improve | Opportunities, Site audit, Backlinks |
| Visibility | AI visibility, Local |
| Manage | Reports, Settings |

On a narrow screen, the active group opens automatically. Expand another group to choose a tool. The current tool stays highlighted. The theme button switches between light and dark mode; your installation's branding remains in place.

## Exporting the Pages library

In **Research → Pages**, apply the URL search and sort order, then choose **Export all matching URLs** to download every matching URL across pagination. Up to 10,000 matching URLs download immediately. For larger selections, up to 200,000 URLs, choose **Prepare CSV export**: background tasks write the file in the selected sort order, and it appears under **Prepared exports** with a **Download CSV** link when ready. A project prepares one export at a time, and prepared files are deleted after 24 hours. Selections above 200,000 URLs must be narrowed; the application never returns a truncated file. **Export this page as CSV** downloads only the current page.

Both exports include Google clicks/impressions, Bing clicks and the search period dates. Empty metric cells mean no imported data; zero remains zero. Bing figures use weekly buckets ending in the shown period. Exports read stored data and do not start provider requests.

## Reading the project Overview

The Overview reads from top to bottom.

1. **KPI row:** Google/Bing clicks, impressions, CTR and average position, with a sparkline of the period. When GA4 data is imported, organic sessions, key events and purchase revenue sit in the same row.
2. **Trends & outlook** sits beside **Where to act next**. Where to act next ranks queries by their estimated click gap: the clicks they would gain at the CTR of observed queries in the same position band. It also lists saved findings with their evidence.
3. **Why it changed:** **What moved** separates gaining and losing queries and pages. Beside it are **Recent SEO changes**, the ranking buckets and landing-page outcomes. Ranking changes use keywords checked on both dates.
4. **Growth & risks:** audit issues, backlinks, indexing and Core Web Vitals; researched demand; competitor and AI visibility; and local coverage.

Each card leads with its result and shows its observation dates. Open **About this data** at the bottom of a card for its sample, method and limits. Printed pages always show these notes. Sources without saved data appear in one **Not set up yet** strip, with a link to set them up. Opening Overview does not run an import or paid lookup.

All signed-in pages use the full width of the screen. Settings, account and project management pages place short form cards side by side; tables keep the full width.

The improved **Performance prognosis** uses up to 180 stored Google Search Console days, independently of the displayed range. It compares recent averages, linear trends and weekday patterns at the selected 7/14/28-day horizon. The validation table shows historical mean absolute error and test samples; **Compared forecast models** lists the competing errors. Four shared weekly origins are needed to select a tested method. A short-history fallback is explicitly unvalidated; sparse or stale data can suppress a forecast. Bing remains in the search summary, rather than mixing incomplete engine coverage in this forecast. Above the chart, one sentence says where each metric is heading at the chosen horizon compared with the average of the last 7 recorded days. Choose one metric to see a shaded error band: for each day ahead, 80% of past backtest forecasts fell inside it; it needs eight backtests per day and ends at the range shown in the metric's tile. The axis follows the recorded and projected values; when the band is wider, it is cut off at the chart edge and the line below the chart says so. The position axis starts at 1. **7-day average** draws recorded and projected lines as trailing 7-day averages, which smooths weekday swings; it leaves out the latest not-final days and the error band. When Google has preliminary numbers for the days after the last final day, each line continues as a dotted segment with a dot per day, so you can see whether the latest days follow the projected trend. A day Google is still collecting (always including today in Pacific time) is not drawn, because its totals are partial; hover it to read them. Hover a day to compare the estimate with the preliminary value; moving the pointer away returns to the last recorded day. Position is drawn upside down, so higher is better on every line. Recorded changes on consecutive days appear as one shaded band. Preliminary numbers never train the forecast. On **Forecasts**, Discover, Google News, News tab, image and video clicks get their own saved series when the site had clicks there in the last 28 days and the history is long enough.

The impressions × CTR click model is used only when it lowers historical error by at least 5% against the linear-click baseline; otherwise the baseline is retained. With short history the compound estimate is explicitly unvalidated. Additional Google position and impression history are tested as CTR inputs, using predicted future inputs rather than future actual measurements. An input needs at least 5% lower historical error on four shared origins before it is used. Endpoint error ranges need eight origins and show historical errors, not guaranteed probability coverage. Overlapping tests are not independent; neither audits nor planned SEO work automatically increase the prediction.

Only complete comparable imports support period deltas. An absent query is not treated as zero. GA4 engagement is not stored; key events per session can exceed one and do not represent a user conversion rate. The CTR gap assumes the observed peer CTR is attainable, rather than promising additional traffic. Changes shown next to metric movement do not prove causation. Missing CrUX coverage is not a passing speed result.

## Finding and comparing rows

**Pages** searches all known URLs for the project. Enter part of a URL or path, choose a sort order and 25, 50 or 100 URLs per page, then select **Apply filters**. Traffic sorts use the imported period shown above the table. Previous and Next retain your filters. Reset clears them. A dash means no imported measurement.

Other read-only tables with eight or more loaded rows offer **Filter loaded rows**, **Sort loaded rows** and **Rows per view**. These work immediately on the rows already delivered to your browser. They do not search records on another server page. Use the report's main filters and pagination to change which records are loaded. The count below the table states how many loaded rows match your filter.

Tables with bulk-selection checkboxes retain their existing filters and selection controls, so adding local pagination cannot hide a selected row. Small tables remain simple. Wide tables scroll horizontally within their card; keyboard users can focus the table region and use the arrow keys.

## Understanding charts and statistics

On **Keywords**, expand **Add keywords** for manual entry or **Suggestions from Search Console** to select imported queries. Entry opens automatically when there are no tracked keywords or when submitted values need correcting. Keeping these sections closed makes the tracked list easier to reach.

The **?** icon beside a section heading explains what its data means, its coverage or how to use the section. Open it with a click or keyboard activation. Escape closes it and returns focus to the help control. Help text does not contact an AI or external provider.

Line charts display their first, latest and highest values. Ranking charts show the best displayed position because lower positions are better.
