These describe the displayed series; use the report's coverage notices to understand its imported data. Focus the chart and use Left/Right to inspect individual points, or expand **View underlying data** for a table of the figures. Date ranges and server-side report filters continue to control the report as before.

## Recording and reviewing SEO changes

Open **Manage → Change timeline** in a project to record dated title, content, link, technical or release changes. Leave the URL blank for a site-wide note or enter an exact project URL. The timeline has date/URL filters and pagination; authorized editors can edit and remove notes. Overview, Google/Bing performance and keyword-history charts show recorded dates with an expandable context list. Read [SEO change annotations](19-seo-change-annotations.md) for limits, permissions and careful interpretation.

## Keeping your installation current

From **Overview → Save forecasts and review actual outcomes**, choose 7, 14 or 28 days and review the stored-data predictions for the site, sampled queries/pages and GA4 organic outcomes. Project editors can save eligible predictions and start weekly tracking, with a pause control. Cron checks outcomes daily and issues all three horizons every seven days using saved data. Original predictions stay fixed when later imports arrive; accepted actuals are saved so they survive source-history retention. Revisit to see actuals and errors. The review page labels its server-generated methods separately from the Overview chart.

The review reads up to 486 stored dates and requires sufficient observed history. Annual patterns and dated calendar assistance compete only when comparable tests support them. Record exact holiday/event occurrences with the same name for comparable events; SEOcc does not guess dates or assume traffic gains. Newly entered dates cannot affect earlier backtests. Forward ranges stay unavailable until 20 completed disjoint forecasts exist for the same source, method and horizon; their empirical 80% target is not guaranteed future coverage. Missing or restricted GA4 data stays unavailable.

Download new versions from the project's GitHub releases and upload them under **System → Updates**. Nothing is installed automatically.

Before clicking **Install**, back up the database and application files through SEOcc and your hosting panel, keep an offline encryption-key backup, and check the backup acknowledgment. SEOcc's automatic database backup is additional protection, not a complete hosting backup.


## Connecting providers

Open **Integrations**, choose a provider's settings and expand its **step-by-step guide**. Each guide explains what you need, the provider setup, what to enter in SEOcc, how to verify the connection and common errors. Installation-wide Google OAuth setup is under **System → Google app**. Project settings contain Search Console/Bing links and IndexNow; Analytics contains the GA4 property link.

Saving a CrUX key does not verify it. Request a check for a known URL, allow cron to run, and inspect its result. A 403 usually requires checking the Cloud project's enabled API and the key's restrictions. “No data” means the exact URL lacks sufficient eligible field data; it does not mean the URL passes Core Web Vitals. Follow the guide before retrying a failed job.

SEOcc keeps the existing role permissions, credential encryption and provider budgets. Tutorials never start a provider request automatically. Read the form's instructions before saving: on CrUX and GA4, a blank credential removes the connection, while some other forms keep an existing secret when left blank.

### Reviewing opportunity coverage

Open Data coverage at the last analysis before acting on SEO findings. Each source shows available, stale or missing and its latest observation date. Old findings stay open when the engine cannot safely recheck them; their scores stay unchanged. Refresh the relevant integration using its existing controls, then analyze again. Analysis itself reads local data and purchases no provider data.

### Opportunity score evidence

Opportunities show the calibrated CTR sample, confidence contributions, impact formula and any stored GA4 key-event/revenue assumptions. Missing or stale inputs remain unknown. Coverage includes top-N-of-total Google samples; unseen findings stay open when a sample is truncated. Declines include a significance check, three-period context and seasonal context when complete monthly history exists. GA4 estimates use stored Organic Search sessions, are correlations, and are not promises of causal conversions. Device/query CTR samples and outcome calibration are not yet available.


Opportunities also use stored query/URL shares and position flips to identify overlapping visibility, successful URL Inspection snapshots to flag indexing concerns, and a complete bounded audit graph to suggest contextual internal links. Multiple ranking URLs alone are not a cannibalization finding. Failed, missing or stale inspections do not prove absence from Google. Internal-link suggestions require an audited indexable source and are withheld above 2,000 pages or 5,000 graph links. Audit traffic/value sums distinct affected URLs across stored rows rather than three examples; missing rows remain unknown. Page and origin CrUX measurements remain distinct. Recent relevant annotations and title/canonical/noindex watch changes apply one −15 confidence adjustment with “measure before acting” evidence and the existing annotation impact comparison. Alert context links existing alerts without creating or sending messages. All analysis uses local records, with no provider request. Per-keyword and per-URL freshness protects old findings even when other records in the same source are fresh.


The findings list, CSV export and MCP list consolidate a normalized query (case and whitespace) or landing page (host/path, trailing slash and query-string variants) into one primary finding, chosen by priority with a stable UUID tie-break. Other rule observations and actions remain supporting evidence. Existing stored subject hashes, UUIDs, tasks and status histories are retained: done/dismissed decisions suppress duplicate open findings for the same canonical subject. The catalog is bounded at 5,000 stored rows; an incomplete catalog withholds open groups rather than overlook closed decisions. Page action plans are available at `/opportunities/by-page` and the scoped read-only `/opportunities/page-plans` endpoint, up to 200 plans. Structured monthly click estimates are nullable; old rows remain unknown until reanalyzed. Page plans take the larger of summed distinct primary-query estimates and the page estimate, instead of adding overlapping page/query gains. This is a scenario estimate, not a causal forecast.


Effort is refined from observable scope: 2–10 touched URLs imply at least medium effort, more than ten high; content work above 1,500 words is at least medium and above 3,000 high; known keyword difficulty ≥30 is medium and ≥60 high. Unknowns retain the rule estimate rather than imply easy work. Fresh stored noindex/canonical or inspection concerns appear as prerequisites before visibility/content work; dependent work follows unblocked findings, then numeric priority, then stable UUID. Priority arithmetic remains impact × confidence / 100 / effort. Time-to-value ranges (near 1–4 weeks, medium 4–8, longer 8–12+) are planning assumptions, not promised effects. `/opportunities/weekly` and the scoped `/opportunities/weekly-plan` read endpoint show up to ten findings with at most three per primary type. MCP `opportunities_list` accepts `view: weekly` and returns the same bounded selection and ordering reasons. A sparse type mix can produce fewer than ten items.


Marking a task or finding done captures a nullable Google baseline for the preceding 28 Pacific calendar days, excluding completion day, and creates scoped UUID outcomes for days 28 and 56. Task/finding completion on the same date shares one idempotent episode; the first baseline is preserved and linked annotations provide context. At day 28, days 1–28 are measured; day 56 measures days 29–56. All 28 import marks and an observed subject are required; missing data retries later, never becomes zero. Non-query/non-page technical findings remain unmeasurable from stored GSC. An hourly local job at :43 handles at most twenty due checkpoints, rotates missing rows, and retries them once per UTC day; due dates use Pacific labels with two days for GSC availability. No providers are called. The comparison widget `/opportunities/outcomes` shows raw baseline/actual clicks, position, CTR and monthly-normalized change, explicitly as correlation.

Project/type realization factors use eligible 56-day completions from the last year, at least five samples and at least 200 impressions in each window. Individual observed monthly change / raw predicted gain ratios are clipped 0–2 and blended with ten neutral prior observations; the final factor is bounded 0.25–1.5. Raw and calibrated predictions are stored separately so calibration does not compound. Technical exposure and unknown gains are not calibrated as incremental gain. Factor, sample count, raw estimate and adjusted estimate appear in evidence and MCP. Outcomes do not isolate implementation effects from seasonality, demand, ranking changes or other edits.


Opportunity detail pages expose numeric priority arithmetic, calibration/value formulas, confidence reasons, source dates, nullable raw/adjusted click estimates and related findings. Read-only JSON detail is at `/opportunities/{finding_uuid}/data`, with normal project authorization and foreign-project/finding 404s. UI and CSV share filters `type`, `page_url` (exact normalized URL/path), `min_impact` (0–100), `effort` (1–3), and `data_basis`. MCP `opportunities_list` accepts those filters, `view: weekly`, optional `opportunity_id` for scoped detail, and `status: snoozed`; these reads use opportunities:read and selected-project constraints. Status changes over MCP need the separate opportunities:write permission (chapter 8). Result-size limits still apply.

Editors can snooze a finding through its detail page until a valid project-local date after today and within one year. This hides equivalent open findings, preserves UUID/history and records an audit event. At the next local analysis on/after that date (normally within the six-hour schedule), a bulk system history transition reopens it; missing sources continue to preserve the finding. A complete fresh analysis can resolve a disappeared condition. Reopening/done/dismissed clears the snooze date. No new provider calls or MCP write scope are introduced.

19.title: SEO change annotations
19.text:
# SEO change annotations

Record what you changed on your website so that your next SEO review has a reliable timeline. An annotation is a manually recorded note, not a measurement or proof that a change caused a result.

## Record a change

1. Open your project, then **Manage → Change timeline**.
2. Choose the actual change date in UTC. Dates can run from 1 January 2000 through today; future changes belong in your work plan rather than this history.
3. Choose Title / snippet, Content update, Internal links, Technical change, Website release or Other.
4. Give the change a short, specific title, such as “Clarified delivery information in the coffee category title”. Titles allow up to 120 characters.
5. Optionally enter the exact HTTP(S) page URL. It must belong to the project domain or its www equivalent. Leave it blank for a site-wide change. Paths and query strings are case-sensitive; fragments, credentials and custom ports are not accepted.
6. Add details if useful: what changed, why, and what you intend to review. Details allow up to 2,000 characters.
7. Keep **Measure this change** ticked for a page change, then save the annotation. SEOcc drafts a measurement plan and freezes its baseline right away:
   - metric: Google clicks for the page, or its CTR for a title or snippet change;
   - comparison: 28 days before and 28 days after the change.

   Its result appears once 28 days of data after the change are imported. Untick the box for a change you do not want measured. A site-wide change has no page to measure, and editing a change never drafts a plan. See *SEO change impact → Measurement plan* to adjust the plan.

Use the date and URL filters (under **Filter by date or page**) to find previous changes. The timeline shows 25 notes per page, newest change date first, grouped by month.

## Follow each change

The counters at the top show how many changes are recorded, how many are **waiting for a recrawl**, how many are **in the effect window** and how many are **ready to review**. Changes older than 120 days count as settled.

Each change has a countdown with the day since the change and a track. The highlighted part of the track is the window in which changes of that type usually start to show in search data:

| Change type | Usually shows | Watch |
|---|---|---|
| Title / snippet | day 7–21 | CTR and clicks |
| Content update | day 14–42 | Impressions and average position |
| Internal links | day 14–56 | Position of the linked pages |
| Technical change | day 3–28 | Indexed pages, impressions and errors |
| Website release | day 7–56 | Site-wide clicks and impressions |
| Other | day 14–42 | Clicks and impressions |

These windows are planning guidance from typical recrawl times, not a prediction for your site. The countdown also gives the date of the full 28-day before/after comparison, which **Review impact** shows once 28 full days have passed.

After 7 days of imported Google data following the change, an **early read** appears. It compares equal, complete periods before and after the change day, up to 28 days each, for clicks, impressions, CTR and average position. It covers the exact page for a page change and the whole site for a site-wide change. Green and orange mark the direction, with lower position counting as better. Changes under 1 % (0.05 points of CTR, 0.1 positions) stay neutral. If either period is incomplete, the early read says so instead of comparing. Filtering by a URL also includes site-wide changes. Authorized project editors can edit or remove notes; viewers can read them. Removing a note hides it from the timeline and context, while the database retains the deleted row and the audit log records the action.

## Change bundles: review, guard and verify an edit

For an edit that should be reviewed before it goes live, use **Manage → Change bundles**. SEOcc never edits your site; you deploy in your CMS.

1. **Draft.** Enter:
   - the page and the problem;
   - the evidence (sources, figures);
   - each exact edit, with what the page says now and the new text;
   - what you expect and how to validate it.
2. **Capture live baseline.** Cron reads the page as it is now: status, title, description, headings, canonical, noindex, word count and body text.
3. **Approve.** The approval covers this exact content and baseline, identified by a hash. Editing the bundle or capturing a new baseline clears the approval.
4. **Check the live page (version guard).** Just before you deploy, SEOcc reads the page again. A deployment can only be recorded after a check from the last 24 hours that matches the approved baseline. If someone changed the page since the approval, SEOcc blocks the record and lists what changed. Capture a new baseline, review the edits against it, and approve again.
5. **Record deployment.** Make the edits in your CMS, then tick the ones that were applied. A partial deployment is kept as such, with a note on what failed. The deployment is added to this change timeline, where the change impact and its measurement plan follow.
6. **Verify on the live page.** SEOcc reads the title, description, main heading, canonical and noindex back and marks each edit *Live* or *Not live*. Body text, redirects and other edits need a check by hand.
7. **Rollback.** If you undo the edits, record when and why. The rollback is also added to the timeline.

Every step is kept in the bundle's history. A bundle that was never deployed can be deleted with its history (*Delete bundle*); a deployed bundle stays as the record of what changed. Viewers can read bundles; editors make and approve them. The MCP `change_bundles` tool gives AI assistants the same read-only view.

## Review the chart context

The project overview, Google and Bing performance charts, and individual keyword history charts show dashed markers for recorded dates within the chart's displayed data. Open **SEO change context** below the chart to read the notes. Several notes on the same date share one marker. Context includes the most recent 100 notes within the selected dates; use the full timeline for older notes or pagination.

Markers follow the existing chart's date positions. On sparse keyword checks, a marker between two checks indicates the change date; it does not invent a ranking measurement for that date. A chart with no data has no markers.

Page details include notes for that exact URL and site-wide changes within the page's reporting period. Recording an annotation does not fetch a URL, modify your website, start a provider request or change an opportunity's status.

## Ask AI about changes

For example: “What changed on this page during the displayed period? Compare the recorded changes with the available traffic and ranking evidence, and tell me what we still cannot conclude.”

Ask AI can read these notes through `annotations_list` and `page_details`. External MCP clients use the existing `projects:read` scope for `annotations_list`; page details still require `pages:read`. These tools are read-only and enforce the user's project access. An MCP client with the **Change notes** permission can also add and edit notes (`annotation_create`, `annotation_update`); such notes show "Last changed via <token name>". Ask AI does not write notes.

Notes are visible to authorized project users and can be included in AI conversations that request this context. Do not put passwords, API keys or other secrets in them. The assistant treats note text as evidence, not instructions.

## Interpret results carefully

Search engines may take time to recrawl and reflect an edit. Seasonality, campaigns, competitors, algorithm changes and missing imports can affect the same period. Annotation dates use UTC; Search Console and other sources can use different date boundaries. Compare complete reporting periods, check data coverage and inspect the affected queries. A marker beside a traffic increase does not establish that your edit caused the increase.

20.title: 20. Brand-name mentions in AI answers
20.text:
# 20. Brand-name mentions in AI answers

An AI answer can name your business without linking to your website. **Project → AI visibility → Brand-name mentions** checks the public name separately from the domain-based results above it.

## Set up your name

1. Connect DataForSEO in **Integrations** and set workspace spending limits. This is a paid provider feature.
2. Open **Brand settings**. Enter the name your customers recognise, up to 120 characters. Prefer a distinctive name; a common name can match unrelated businesses.
3. Choose the Google country and language. ChatGPT results always cover the United States in English, regardless of this choice.
4. Leave weekly checks off for manual control, or explicitly tick the weekly paid-check option.
5. Select **Save brand settings**. Saving alone makes no provider request. With weekly checks enabled, the next eligible cron run starts a check and subsequent checks run at least seven days after the last attempt.
6. Select **Check brand name** for a manual check. It uses four requests: a count and up to 25 answer examples for each platform. The current estimate is about **$0.452**; actual provider charges are recorded under spending, and workspace budgets apply to every request.

Cron processes one request per job. Refreshing this page and reading saved results do not start another paid lookup. The same check cannot be queued twice while it is pending.

## Understand the results

- **Name mentions** counts provider word matches in answer text. Matching can contain additional words; it is not an exact-phrase guarantee.
- **AI search volume** is the provider's estimated monthly question volume, not visits or sales. “Unavailable” means the provider did not supply it.
- **Answer examples** contain a short excerpt, question, provider response date and cited sources. A brand mention can have **no project-domain citation**. If your domain appears among the sources, its source rank is shown separately.
- **History** shows the latest 12 attempts for the same name, market and project domain. The charts use the latest completed check per UTC day. Failed and missing checks are not zero. Changing the name or market selects a separate series; previous checks remain stored.

Read the excerpts to reject namesakes. These are samples from DataForSEO's ChatGPT and Google AI database, not a complete record of every AI conversation, website, news article or social mention. Gemini and Perplexity are not included.

**Do not add brand-name counts to domain counts.** The same answer can match both. Compare each series with itself and consider other evidence before attributing a change to SEO work.

## Failures and stopping checks

Provider or budget failures retain the attempt's status and do not replace a previous completed result with partial data. A failed check is not automatically retried. Weekly opt-in can start a fresh check after seven days; switch it off to stop that schedule.

If a process stops during a request, SEOcc records the step as processing before sending it and will not automatically resend it. Review **System → Jobs** and provider spending before requesting another paid check. A pending check blocks new checks for 24 hours. After that, an explicit new check supersedes the abandoned one, preventing its late queued steps from making further requests. A request already sent may still be billed.

Untick weekly checks to stop scheduled work. Clear the name and save to stop tracking entirely while retaining stored history. Changed settings or revoked project access stop further queued requests; an already sent request may still be billed.

## Ask AI and ChatGPT

Ask AI can use the saved name results through `ai_visibility`. For example: “Compare Acme Outdoor's completed name-mention checks, identify any namesakes in the excerpts, and distinguish mentions from website citations.” The tool reads saved data and does not spend provider money. External MCP tokens need the existing **rankings:read** scope and access to the project.

21.title: Content briefs
21.text:
# Content briefs

A content brief turns saved SEO evidence into a writing plan. Open **Project → Improve → Content briefs**. Create, edit and remove require project editing permission; viewers can read, print and download briefs.

## Start with evidence

- **Pages → Page details → Create content brief** uses that exact URL’s saved queries, search figures, crawl title/description, issues, possible cannibalization and internal-link candidates.
- **Keywords → Create content brief** uses that tracked keyword’s selected country/language, saved metrics and the newest check within the last 90 days for the project’s configured device. Its saved top ten organic URLs are references to inspect, not analyzed competitor articles. A usable ranked URL becomes the target.
- **Opportunities → Create content brief** retains the selected opportunity’s explanation, evidence and last detection date. A query/keyword and exact page URL are prefilled when available.
- **Content briefs → Create content brief** also works for a new page: enter a target keyword and optionally its planned URL. Use a URL on your project’s domain, without a port, credentials or fragment. A page absent from the stored catalog has no page evidence yet.

Creating or saving a brief performs no provider request or crawl and is free. Connecting integrations is not required to write a manual brief. Source dates can differ, and missing data is unavailable, not zero.

## Review the writing plan

Choose the target keyword and audience, classify the search intent, and edit the title, meta description, heading outline, topics, internal links and writer instructions. Existing crawl snippets are starting values. The initial outline is a generic editable scaffold; intent is deliberately **unclassified**. SEOcc does not invent competitor headings or claim to have analyzed content it has not collected.

Related queries are the first 20 stored page query rows, not a complete keyword universe. Google hides anonymized queries. Link candidates depend on the latest bounded crawl, relevance, indexability and eligible terms near the top. Possible cannibalization requires human judgment: several URLs can serve different intents.

The original evidence is captured on save, capped at 85 lines/30 KB with at most 2,500 characters per line, and stays unchanged when the brief’s target or text is edited. It includes the original target and source dates. Clearing a prefilled target URL plans a new page and does not silently capture the old page’s snapshot. Create a new brief for a fresh snapshot; review current Pages and Rankings before acting. Source omissions and limits stay visible.

## Check claims against sources

Under **Claims and sources** on a brief, list each factual claim the article will make, such as a germination rate, a flowering time or a yield. For each claim, record:
- the exact wording;
- the content or product it appears in;
- what the claim is about: breeder or brand, cultivar or product, product version, market;
- the source you checked: address, publisher, date checked, and the supporting passage or where it is (page, table, section);
- what the source itself is about, including a research sample;
- your verdict: *Unreviewed*, *Supported*, *Partly supported*, *Contradicted*, *Outdated* or *Unverifiable*, with a note.

The verdict is always yours. SEOcc's **automated checks** sit next to it and only point at what to look at:
- a source about another breeder, cultivar, version, market or sample than the claim (one breeder's specification does not carry over to another breeder's product);
- a competitor or your own site as the source (not independent validation);
- no source;
- *Supported* without a passage;
- a source whose scope is not recorded;
- a check older than a year.

"Brandywine #33" and "Brandywine" count as the same cultivar (a phenotype number); "Brandywine Auto" or "Brandywine Cake Ice" do not.

Edits are versioned: two people cannot overwrite each other. If you change the claim or its evidence but leave the verdict as it was, the verdict goes back to *Unreviewed*, because it was given for different evidence. Every earlier version is kept under **History**. SEOcc never rewrites a claim or publishes anything.

## Ask AI and share with a writer

On a saved brief, **Ask AI to improve this brief** asks the existing assistant to read it and propose edits. The assistant must be configured; normal model costs, permissions and budgets apply. Copy reviewed suggestions into the editor and save them yourself. There is no AI write tool or automatic publishing.

**Download text** returns a UTF-8 `.txt` copy with instructions and original evidence. **Printable view** supports your browser’s Print / Save as PDF command. Server-generated or scheduled PDF attachments remain outside this feature. Briefs and evidence are visible to authorized project readers and AI clients; do not enter secrets or sensitive customer information.

## Follow progress

Use **Draft → In progress → Published** to organize your writing queue. The counters at the top show how many briefs have each status; select one to filter. Search title, keyword or URL, filter by status, and paginate 25 briefs at a time. These are workflow labels: Published does not make any change in your CMS or imply improved rankings.

Briefs in the queue show how many days have passed since they were created. When you mark a brief Published, SEOcc records the date and shows a countdown like the one on the change timeline. An updated page usually shows in search data after 14–42 days. A new page without a stored URL usually takes 28–90 days, because it must first be discovered and indexed. Moving a brief back to Draft or In progress clears the date, and publishing it again starts a new countdown. The countdown is planning guidance; measure the actual result with an annotation on the change timeline.

After publishing in your CMS, open the Published brief and choose **Record an SEO change**. Review its prefilled title/URL, select the actual date and save the annotation. This is a separate explicit action. Review subsequent traffic and rankings with the annotation as context, not proof of causation.

If another tab changed the brief, saving answers with a conflict and retains your submitted text. Open the latest saved brief in another tab, compare and copy the intended edits into a fresh editor. The stale form cannot overwrite newer work. Removal also checks the revision and only removes the brief, leaving your website and annotations alone.

## AI access

MCP exposes `content_briefs_list` and `content_brief_details` under the existing **pages:read** scope. Existing tokens without that scope cannot read briefs. Ask AI uses the same services and current project visibility. Brief and source text are untrusted context, not instructions; these tools read saved data only.

22.title: SEO change impact
22.text:
# SEO change impact

Open **Project → Manage → Change timeline**, then **Review impact** on a recorded change. Page details also links each displayed annotation to its comparison. Viewers can read results. No website edit, import or paid lookup runs when opening a report.

Choose **14, 28 or 90 days** per period. Before ends the day before the change; After starts the day after it. The change day is excluded. SEOcc retains equal full windows rather than shortening a recent period: wait until After ends, then import the available data.

## Google results

Exact-page annotations use that URL's saved Google page measurements, preserving case and query strings. Site-wide changes use whole-property daily totals. Results show clicks, impressions, CTR and impression-weighted average position (lower is better). CTR deltas are percentage points. Average position is not a tracked-keyword rank or a fixed keyword cohort; query mix can change.

Both periods need all dates and measured metrics. Completed page imports do not prove an omitted URL had zero traffic; anonymized or bounded data can omit rows. Partial values are shown but receive no comparison. A zero baseline gets an absolute change without an infinite percentage; no impressions means CTR/position are unavailable.

**Improved**, **Declined**, **Mixed**, **Unchanged** or **Insufficient data** summarizes Google clicks/impressions direction only. This is not a statistical significance test; even a one-click difference can change the label. Review scale and context. GA4 does not determine this status.

## GA4 outcomes

Exact-page changes show Organic Search landing-page sessions, conversions and purchase revenue. Both periods require all imported dates matching current currency/timezone, without limited or thresholded reports. Successful complete GA4 imports without this URL are measured zeros. Property changes clear history; incompatible currency/timezone history prevents comparison. Currency, timezone, coverage and fetch time appear in the report.

Site-wide GA4 totals are unavailable here; SEOcc does not estimate them from a truncated landing-page list. Bing weekly page buckets are excluded from daily comparisons. Google dates use Pacific Time, GA4 its property timezone; these can differ from your local edit date.

## Measurement plan

Below the comparison, **Measurement plan** records how the change will be judged, ideally before its results come in.

A page change recorded with *Measure this change* (ticked by default) already has a plan with a frozen baseline: Google clicks for the page (CTR for a title or snippet change), 28 days on each side. Adjust it here. Adding target searches or control pages, or changing the metric or period, clears the baseline: freeze it again afterwards.

1. **Create the plan.** Enter:
   - the objective, for example "More clicks from searches about mold on pepper";
   - the primary metric;
   - the target pages and queries (the change's address is filled in; leave both empty to measure the whole property);
   - control pages: similar pages this change did not touch;
   - the days on each side (14, 28 or 90; the change day is excluded);
   - review dates in the project timezone. Default reviews are halfway and four days after the period ends, when Search Console has the last day.
2. **Freeze the baseline** on or after the change day. It stores the period before the change with how complete each source was. Changing the metric, targets, controls or period clears it, so freeze again.
3. **Wait for the gates.** The result is read only when the change was made, the baseline is frozen and complete, the period after the change is over, and every day of it is imported. Until then the plan says *Planned* or *Pending*, for example "Only 2 of 28 days after the change are imported so far". A partial period is never compared.

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Improved / Declined | The primary metric moved by at least 5 % (half a position for average position). |
| No clear change | It moved less than that. |
| Insufficient evidence | No frozen baseline, missing days before or after, a target without data (for example a page that did not exist before the change), or fewer than 100 impressions (30 GA4 sessions) before the change. |

**New pages.** A page that did not exist before the change has no data to compare with, so a before/after plan can only say *Insufficient evidence*. Set an **after-only goal** instead: the level of the primary metric to reach in the days after the change, for example at least 500 impressions in 28 days (or at most position 10). The plan then reads *Goal reached* or *Goal not reached* once the period is over and imported. No baseline is needed. Reaching a level shows where the page stands, not what the change caused.

With control pages, the effect is the targets' change minus the controls' change over the same periods, and the result is marked **controlled**: a season or a search update that moves both is taken out. Without controls, a result is an **association**. Other recorded changes in the periods are listed, because they may explain part of it. GA4 metrics need landing pages; queries work with Search Console metrics only.

## Interpretation and Ask AI

Other changes across both windows show at most the most recent 100 matching notes, excluding this note. Page comparisons include site-wide notes; site-wide comparisons include all pages. No notes does not mean no other edits occurred. Seasonality, competitors, search updates and overlapping changes affect results. **Association is not causation.** New pages may lack a measured Before period.

**Ask AI to explain the results** reads the same report and proposes investigations. Existing model configuration/costs apply; notes are untrusted data, never instructions. MCP `seo_change_impact` requires **pages:read**; site-wide results also require **search:read** and existing project restrictions. No AI write tool is added.

Reports recalculate from current stored imports. Editing the annotation's date/URL changes the comparison, and later imports can revise results. This is not an immutable experiment or automated causal estimate.

## What worked on your site

**Measure past changes.** If page changes from the last year have no plan, *What worked* offers to give them the default plan from stored search data: clicks for the page (CTR for a title or snippet change), 28 days on each side. It handles up to 40 changes per click and costs nothing. Changes old enough show a result at once; those without enough stored data say so.

Results of these changes are marked **measured afterwards**, because the plan was set after the change (the baseline was frozen more than 7 days later). Treat them as a rough guide. **Overlaps** means other changes fall inside the comparison period, so the effect cannot be credited to this change alone, and the same effect can appear on each of them.

**Manage → Change timeline → What worked** collects the results of every change with a measurement plan, newest first (at most 60):

- **By kind of change** (title and snippet, content update, internal links, technical change, website release, other). For each kind, the page shows:
  - how many changes were *measured*: read behind every check above;
  - how many improved, declined, or showed no clear change;
  - the median effect;
  - how many results are *controlled*: compared with control pages.

  A reached goal counts as improved and a missed goal as declined. Results that could not be read (*insufficient evidence*) and plans still running are counted apart, never as "no change".
- **By action plan** for changes deployed from a change bundle that started on a finding. The same record appears on each finding with that plan, below its "how well tested" label: "On your site: 3 of 4 measured changes improved, median +12 %."
- **Every measured change** with its metric, result and effect. Effects are "better is positive": percent for clicks, impressions, CTR, sessions and key events; positions gained for average position.
- **To make results readable**: plans without a frozen baseline, and changes to a page from the last 180 days without a measurement plan.

Fewer than three measured changes of a kind are too few to show a pattern. Uncontrolled results are associations, not causes. MCP `what_worked` (**pages:read**) returns the same summary.

23.title: Google indexing monitoring
23.text:
# Google indexing monitoring

Use **Project → Visibility → Google indexing** to see what Google last reported about an important URL. This helps investigate a page that stopped receiving traffic, a redirected page or an unexpected canonical.

## Connect Google once

1. Follow [Connecting Google Search Console](05-google-search-console.md). Enable **Google Search Console API** in the same Google Cloud project as your existing integration.
2. Connect your Google account under **Integrations**. Your account must have access to the relevant Search Console property.
3. Link that property under the project's **Settings**. Domain properties cover their subdomains; a URL-prefix property covers only its exact protocol, hostname and path prefix.

The existing read-only Search Console permission is sufficient. There is no separate API key, CrUX key or additional OAuth permission for indexing checks.

## Inspect an important page

1. Open **Google indexing**, or use **Inspect or watch this URL** in Page details.
2. Enter the exact HTTP(S) URL on your project's domain. Keep the original path and query-string capitalization. URLs with credentials, ports or fragments are rejected.
3. Choose **Request Google check**. Your hosting cron processes the queued request. Refresh later to see the saved result.
4. Expand **Review saved Google evidence**. The successful-check time says when SEOcc received the result; **Last Google crawl** says when Google reported crawling the page. They are different timestamps, shown in UTC.

Google's API returns its **stored index version**, which can lag changes on your website. It does not run a live page test, request indexing or edit your website. For a live test or an indexing request, use Google Search Console yourself.

## Read the evidence correctly

| State | What it means |
|---|---|
| Reported indexed | Google returned a PASS verdict at the saved check time. |
| Indexing concern | Google returned FAIL, PARTIAL or NEUTRAL. Read its coverage description before deciding what to fix. |
| Unchecked | No successful result is saved. This does not mean the URL is absent from Google. |
| Older than 14 days | The last successful result is older than two weeks. It can be useful history, but should not be treated as current. |
| Check failed | The latest attempt failed; the last successful evidence remains visible. A failure does not prove deindexing. |
| Unknown verdict | Google did not return a recognized verdict. SEOcc does not infer one. |

Compare **Google-selected canonical** with **User-declared canonical** and the intended page URL. When both are known and differ, the page shows *Google chose a different canonical than the page declares*. A redirect or duplicate can legitimately use a different canonical.

The saved evidence also lists the sitemaps that contain the URL, a sample of up to five pages Google found linking to it, and the **rich results** Google detected (for example product snippets or breadcrumbs) with their errors and warnings. Errors mean that rich result may not show; Google's Rich Results Test gives the details. Combine this with Site audit and your own Search Console investigation. Missing crawl or canonical fields mean **Not reported**, not a confirmed defect.

## Indexing history of one address

Choose **History** next to a saved URL, or open **Google indexing → History** and enter an address. Six states are kept apart, each with its evidence and date:

| State | Comes from |
|---|---|
| Public | The latest completed site audit: an HTTP 2xx answer. A redirect or error is *No*. |
| Technically indexable | Public, no noindex, no canonical to another address, and not blocked by robots.txt in Google's last check. |
| Known to Google | The latest Google check. *URL is unknown to Google* is *No*. |
| Indexed | Only a Google check with a PASS verdict. A recorded request never counts. |
| Request submitted | An indexing request you recorded. |
| Recrawl observed | Google's reported last crawl is after the recorded request. A crawl on the day of the request, before you recorded it, stays *Unknown*, because it may have come first. |

*Unknown* means there is no evidence yet, not that something is wrong. The **timeline** below lists, newest first:
- site audit fetches;
- when SEOcc's IndexNow sitemap check first read the address in your sitemap (it may have been listed earlier, so this is not a publication date);
- IndexNow submissions, which reach Bing, Yandex and others but not Google;
- each Google check, noting verdict and canonical changes;
- the crawls Google reported;
- recorded requests.

Google checks are kept as history from 0.37.0 on, up to 30 per address.

### Record an indexing request

SEOcc never asks Google to index a page and does not use the Indexing API. To make a request:

1. On the history page, open the address in Search Console URL Inspection with the link provided.
2. Choose **Request indexing** there and wait for Google's confirmation.
3. Back in SEOcc, choose how you made the request and the day of the request (in the project timezone). Enter Google's confirmation as evidence, then **Record request**. The address is added to the saved URLs.
4. After a few days, choose **Request Google check**. When Google's last crawl is after the request, *Recrawl observed* becomes *Yes*. *Indexed* changes only with Google's verdict.

Project editors record requests; viewers can read the history.

## Watch priority URLs weekly

Choose **Watch weekly** next to a saved URL. Focus on your homepage, valuable landing pages and pages affected by recent changes. You can watch up to 50 URLs per project. Cron queues up to 50 due URLs per hour across this installation; each watch becomes due seven days after its last request or attempt. A failed check gets the queue's bounded retries, then waits until its next weekly cycle.

Choose **Stop weekly checks** to remove a watch. Its saved evidence stays readable; a request already queued can still finish. Checks are not enabled for every page automatically.

After **two successful checks** report a different indexing verdict or Google-selected canonical, SEOcc records a change alert. The first result and failed checks create no change alert. Control personal delivery under [Notifications](17-alerts-and-digest.md); existing project team delivery also applies. An alert reports a change in evidence, not proof that an SEO edit caused it.

## Filters, limits and troubleshooting

Search exact URL text and filter the inspection list by watchlist, reported state, unchecked, failed or stale evidence, **Google chose another canonical** or **Rich result errors**.

**Sitemaps in Search Console** above the list shows each sitemap of the linked property with submitted URLs, errors, warnings and when Google last read it. It is refreshed with every Search Console import and makes no extra inspection calls. Open Search Console's Sitemaps report for the details of an error. Results are paginated in groups of 25. The list holds at most 500 saved URLs per project; other Pages URLs are not inspected automatically.

Manual requests for one URL are spaced at least ten minutes apart. Conservative local budgets allow 20 provider calls per property per minute and 1,000 per installation per UTC day, including retries. Google's quotas are shared with your other tools and can be reached sooner. See Google's [URL Inspection documentation](https://developers.google.com/webmaster-tools/v1/urlInspection.index/inspect) and [usage limits](https://developers.google.com/webmaster-tools/limits).

- **No result yet:** check that cron runs and review **System → Jobs**. Queued work is not a successful inspection.
- **Google rejected the check:** confirm the API is enabled, the connected account has property access, and the exact URL lies inside that property.
- **Reconnect Google:** restore the connection under Integrations. Failed checks preserve previous results.
- **Local budget reached:** wait and request another check later; avoid repeatedly checking unchanged pages.
- **Property changed:** saved evidence belongs to its original connection/property. Relinking hides old evidence; request a fresh check for the new property. Old queued work is discarded.

Project editors request checks and manage watches. Authorized viewers, Ask AI and MCP clients with `pages:read` can read saved evidence; the MCP `indexing_status` tool also returns the history states and timeline. **Ask AI** can explain coverage and suggest investigations, but it cannot run inspections or alter watches. Its normal configured AI costs apply; the indexing read tool makes no Google call.

24.title: SEO team tasks
24.text:
# SEO team tasks

Turn a detected SEO opportunity into a work plan for your team. Tasks use data already on your server and add no provider costs. They do not edit your website or send reminders.

## Create a task from a finding

Open **Project → Opportunities → SEO findings**, then choose **Manage task** on a finding. Its explanation and priority remain visible beside your work plan.

Choose **To do**, **In progress** or **Done**. Assign an active member who has edit access to this project, optionally set a due date and exact page URL, and add plain-text work notes. Save the task to add it to **Opportunities → Team tasks**. One finding has one task; opening it again edits the existing plan.

Due dates use the project's timezone. An unfinished task becomes overdue on the next local date after its due date. A task due today is not overdue. Stored update timestamps are UTC. Authorized viewers can read tasks; project editors can save them. Members who lose edit access or leave the workspace appear as unavailable and should be reassigned. Assignment never grants project access.

## Find the next piece of work

The Team tasks list supports status, assignee, unassigned work, overdue unfinished tasks, minimum finding priority (50 or 75), exact page URL and literal search across titles, work notes and URLs. Results show 25 tasks per page. Unfinished work comes first, then earlier due dates and higher finding priority. Filters remain when moving between pages.

The list contains saved task plans only. To plan another finding, return to SEO findings and choose Manage task. Task titles and priorities follow the latest stored finding evidence.

## Keep work status separate from SEO evidence

Task progress describes what your team is doing. The existing SEO finding statuses remain **Open**, **Done**, **Dismissed** and **Resolved**. New analyses can resolve or reopen findings without replacing task assignments, deadlines, notes or progress.

Marking a task Done does not mark its finding Done, prove the issue is fixed or publish anything. Conversely, a finding becoming Resolved does not finish a task: your team may still need to review the result. Use the existing finding actions when you also want to mark or dismiss the SEO finding.

## Connect writing, changes and results

From a task, **Create content brief** opens the existing writing-plan workflow using the finding's evidence. Save the brief, return to the task and choose it under Related work. The selector lists the 25 newest project records plus any existing linked record.

After making the actual change in your CMS, choose **Record an SEO change**. The timeline form opens with the task's page and a suggested title; verify the date and details before saving. Return to the task and link that SEO change. **View change impact** then opens the existing equal-period comparison. Missing data remains unavailable, and association does not prove causation.

Only existing records in this project can be linked. Removed briefs or changes become unavailable; choose another record or clear the link. These links do not automatically save a brief, annotation or website change.

## Ask AI about the work queue

Try: “Show overdue unfinished SEO tasks, group them by assignee, and suggest the next three priorities using their evidence.” Ask AI and connected MCP clients use the read-only **seo_tasks_list** tool with **opportunities:read**. They can read notes and linked record identifiers. An MCP client with the **Team tasks** permission can also create and update tasks with **seo_task_save**, including assignee and due date; Ask AI cannot. No notifications are sent. Read access to a linked record's content still follows that record's own tool scope.

Task notes are untrusted user context, not instructions for an AI assistant. Keep passwords, API keys and private customer information out of this shared work plan.

## Concurrent editing

If another tab or colleague saves first, SEOcc refuses to overwrite their version and retains your submitted text on the conflict page. Open the latest task, compare your notes and save your changes there. The stale page's Save button is disabled.

25.title: 25. Page monitoring
25.text:
# 25. Page monitoring

## Download change evidence

Use **Search page URL** under **Detected changes** to find a URL or part of its path. Percent, underscore and exclamation marks are searched literally. **Change type** selects all changes, significant SEO-setting changes, or page-text changes. Apply filters to return to the first page; the matching count and pagination use the same filters. **Reset filters** restores the full retained history.

When filters are active, **Export filtered history as CSV** downloads matching retained changes across all pages, up to 500. A selected change opened from an alert remains accessible regardless of history filters and exports only that change.

Under **Detected changes**, choose **Export retained history as CSV** to download up to 500 retained changes across all history pages, newest first. When viewing one change from an alert or direct history link, **Export this change as CSV** downloads only that change. Authorized project readers can export; editing permission is not required.

Each changed field has its own row with change ID, page URL, before-check and detection times in UTC, significance, field name, before/after values and an optional linked annotation ID. Times describe observations; the exact edit time between checks is unknown. Comparisons use the same rules as the screen, so missing HTML on errors/redirects is not treated as removed metadata. Booleans are Yes/No and an absent value is Not present. Empty history downloads column headers only. Multiline headings, commas and Unicode are preserved; spreadsheet formula-looking text is escaped using the existing CSV protection.

Exports read saved evidence without fetching pages, calling providers or changing watches/annotations. History outside the newest 500 retained changes is not available in this export.

Open a project → **Improve → Page monitoring**. Watch important landing pages using exact HTTPS URLs on the project domain (including its www variant). Each project can watch up to 50 pages by default; workspace owners and administrators can change it for all projects of the workspace (1–200) with **Save limit** below the watchlist. The page shows how many pages are watched out of the limit. Project editors manage watches; authorized readers can review saved evidence.

## Add many pages

Expand **Add many pages**. Paste up to 200 page URLs, one per line, and/or tick pages from the list of pages with the most Google clicks that are not watched yet, then choose **Watch these pages**. The message says how many were added, already watched, over the limit or not on the project domain. When the watchlist is full, the section says so instead. Each new page is read within the hour for its *before* snapshot.

## Change notes get before and after checks

When you record a change note (see [SEO change annotations](19-seo-change-annotations.md)) for an exact page URL on the project domain, SEOcc watches that page if it is not watched yet and the limit allows, reads it right away unless it was read in the last day, and reads it again 3 days later. The change found by those checks can then verify the outcome of a completed opportunity for that page (see [Did the change work?](07-competitors-and-opportunities.md)). Site-wide notes start no checks.

From **Pages → page details**, choose **Monitor this page for weekly SEO changes** to prefill its URL, then explicitly select **Watch weekly**.

## Weekly checks

Choose **Watch weekly**. A new page is read within the hour, then each watch is checked every seven days. The dispatcher queues at most 50 due pages per hour across the installation. One bounded background job checks one page, respecting robots.txt, public-address protections and the existing crawler's response-size limits. Reads and watchlist changes do not fetch the website during the browser request.

The first complete check establishes a baseline and does not create a change alert. Subsequent checks compare the title, meta description, first 20 H1 texts and total H1 count, resolved canonical, noindex (HTML and HTTP header directives), and HTTP status. Text is bounded to the crawler's existing limits. JavaScript-generated content is not rendered; redirects are recorded without following them. Metadata on non-HTML responses is unavailable rather than evidence that a title or canonical was removed.

Robots blocks, network failures and truncated responses retain the last complete evidence and show a check message. An HTTP error response such as 404 or 503 is observed status evidence and can be compared. A stopped watch is no longer checked; its detected change history remains. Re-adding it establishes a new baseline and invalidates old queued work. If the project's domain changes, old watches show a message and must be replaced.

## Before and after

Expand **Latest saved evidence** on a watched page. **Detected changes** shows the values before and after, with the two check timestamps in UTC. History retains the newest 500 changes per project, displayed 25 at a time. The actual website edit time between observations is unknown; an observed change is not proof of an SEO problem or traffic impact.

Canonical, noindex and HTTP status changes count as significant. They feed the existing deduplicated alert system, subject to your personal alert preferences and project access; configured team webhooks use their existing choices. Title, description and H1 changes remain visible in history without sending routine text-change alerts. Under **Notifications**, choose **Important page SEO settings changed** to enable or mute this alert type.

## Record a change and compare impact

Review the detected change and enter the actual edit date if known. The form defaults to the detection date in UTC; comparisons using that date are approximate context. Choose **Record annotation and compare impact** to save an exact-page annotation containing the observation interval and a bounded before/after summary, then open the existing impact comparison.

Repeated clicks reuse the linked annotation rather than creating duplicates. If it was explicitly removed, the action can recreate it. The impact report uses the existing equal 14/28/90-day windows, data coverage checks and Google/GA4 evidence. It may be unavailable until enough time and imported data exist. Association does not prove causation.

No page is edited or published by this feature. It adds no paid provider calls. Existing read-only AI annotation and impact tools can read the annotation after you save it. An MCP client with the **Page watches** permission can start or stop watches with `page_watch_set` (up to 50 URLs per call, within the project limit).

26.title: 26. The Quest Log
26.text:
# 26. The Quest Log

The **Quest Log** teaches SEOcc by having you finish quests on your own website. A quest is complete when SEOcc can see the real work in your data: a connected property, a recorded change, a created brief. Finishing the campaign means your project is fully set up and you have already acted on your first wins.

Open **Quest Log** in the navigation. It is available in every plan.

## Chapters and ranks

The campaign has six chapters. Finishing a chapter earns its rank.

| Chapter | Rank | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Foundations | Navigator | Set up cron, your website, data connections, keywords and rank tracking ([chapter 4](04-first-steps.md)) |
| 2. Reading the Signals | Analyst | Read search performance and rankings, set up alerts, inspect a page in Google |
| 3. Finding Wins | Strategist | Work with opportunities, priority bands, results-page formats and competitors |
| 4. Taking Action | Operator | Write a content brief, turn wins into team tasks, ask the AI assistant |
| 5. Proving Impact | Specialist | Record changes, measure their impact and outcomes, schedule reports |
| 6. Mastery | SEO Lead | Site audit, page monitoring, Bing, Google Analytics, Core Web Vitals, AI tools (MCP), backlinks, local, and the Weekly Check-in |

Each quest explains why it matters, what you will learn, its steps, pro tips (💡), common mistakes (⚠️), roughly how long it takes and the guide chapter to read. **Show me** opens the right page and highlights the place to act with a small hint; press Escape or **Got it** to close it. When the AI assistant is set up, **Ask AI about this quest** opens it with a question about your current step; each question uses your assistant budget.

## How progress works

- **Foundations is live.** Its status always reflects your current settings for the selected website, so a step can go back to **Needs attention**. Your Navigator rank is kept; a "Needs attention" marker appears on Chapter 1 and on the Quest Log card instead.
- **Other quests stay done.** They are checked when you open the Quest Log or its card, and every hour in the background, so waiting steps such as "first report delivered" finish on their own. Once complete, a quest stays complete even if the data changes later.
- **Your own work counts.** Where SEOcc records who did something (a change, a brief, a competitor, an opportunity status), the quest looks for your own work. Learning quests count work on any project you can see in the workspace; progress is per person and per workspace.
- **Only what you can use is shown.** Quests for features turned off on this installation, or for work your role can't do, are left out. Chapter progress counts only the quests you see, so every plan can reach 100 %. When your license gains features, **New quests available** lists the additions; ranks you earned are kept.
- **Waiting steps** (⏳) depend on background work, such as the first import or a measured outcome. You don't need to wait on the page.

## Skipping and hiding

You can skip any quest outside Foundations; a skipped quest counts as resolved and you can bring it back from its page. Foundations steps can't be skipped, because they are your actual setup. Steps your role can't perform are marked **Handled by your administrator**: they keep their live status but don't count against your progress.

**Hide this card** on the dashboard or project overview hides the Quest Log card for you in this workspace. The Quest Log itself stays in the navigation, where **Show it again** brings the card back. There are no forced tours, pop-ups on sign-in, leaderboards or streaks.

## Paid work

Viewing the Quest Log never queues work, calls providers or spends money. Quests that involve paid DataForSEO work (keywords, rank tracking, backlinks, local) say so: review your budget before you start them. Rank tracking is only switched on by you, on the Rankings page.

27.title: 27. Data quality
27.text:
# 27. Data quality

Open **Manage → Data quality** in a project before you compare periods or trust a number. The page reads only what SEOcc has stored; it never starts an import or a paid lookup.

## Missing is not zero

SEOcc keeps two cases apart:

- **Measured zero:** Google or GA4 reported the day, and there were no clicks, impressions or sessions. That is a real result.
- **Missing:** the day, source or report was never imported completely. Nothing is known about it, so it must not be read as zero.

The same rule applies to Ask AI and to MCP clients, which read this page through the `data_quality` tool.

## What the page shows

- **Status counts:** how many datasets are available, sampled, stale or missing. Each dataset uses the same freshness rule as Opportunities. For example, Search Console is fresh for 7 days and research for 30.
- **Checks:** things to keep in mind before comparing.
  - Days missing from Search Console or GA4.
  - GA4 reports that Google limited or thresholded.
  - Organic sessions without any key events.
  - Timezone differences: Search Console days are Pacific time.
  - Why Google and Bing positions, or GA4 sessions and Search Console clicks, are not the same measure.
- **Import completeness:** for the last 90 imported days of Search Console, how many are complete. Each missing day or range is listed, along with measured zero days and how far behind the newest day is. Bing shows its stored span and lag; Bing data normally ends about three days before today.
- **Google Analytics 4:** whether GA4 is connected, linked and imported, plus the days covered, row limits and privacy thresholds. It also shows whether key events and purchase revenue were recorded. Under **Attribution limits** you can read what GA4 data can and cannot tell you. For example, sessions are credited to the landing page of the session, not to a search query.
- **All datasets:** every source the opportunity engine uses, grouped, with its status, the date its data ends and notes.

## Fixing what it finds

- **Missing days in Search Console:** run the import again under the project settings. Google keeps about 16 months, so older gaps cannot be filled.
- **No key events recorded:** check in GA4 that your important events (purchase, lead, sign-up) are marked as key events. SEOcc cannot see that setting.
- **Limited or thresholded GA4:** compare trends and larger pages; small pages may be missing from the report.
- **Stale research or audits:** start a new run from that module when you need current numbers.

28.title: 28. Investigations
28.text:
# 28. Investigations

An investigation keeps the evidence for one question together: what you are trying to find out, the dated sources you used, the checks you made, what the data cannot show, and your conclusion. Open **Research → Investigations** in a project.

## Start one

Enter what you are investigating (for example *Why did sunflower seed traffic drop in October?*) and, if you like, the question or hypothesis. Project editors can start and change investigations; everyone who sees the project can read them.

You can also start one from a **Why they outrank you** analysis: under the result, choose **Start an investigation with it**.

## Add evidence

Each entry is one of four kinds:

- **Source:** where evidence comes from, with the date it was observed: an analysis, a research lookup, a page or any URL.
- **Check:** something you verified, for example "Compared October with September on the same weekdays".
- **Limitation:** what the data cannot show, for example "GA4 is not linked" or "two competing pages blocked the reader".
- **Note:** anything else worth keeping.

On the investigation page:

- **Analysis** adds a finished *Why they outrank you* analysis with its sources (the results page and each page it read), the checks it made (format, subtopic coverage, bottleneck, internal links) and its limitations (unreadable pages, low confidence, no owner page, no AI explanation, structure only).
- **Lookup on file** adds a stored research lookup from *Research on file* as a dated source, with its market, inputs and whether it is still current.
- The form adds an entry by hand, optionally with a URL and the date the evidence was observed (not in the future).

Adding never buys data: it records what SEO Control Center already stored. An investigation holds up to 300 entries; **Remove** takes one out.

## Conclude

Under **Edit, conclude or archive**, change the title or question, write the conclusion and set the status:

- **Open** while you are still collecting evidence;
- **Concluded** once you have a conclusion (it is required);
- **Archived** when it no longer matters.

If someone else saved the investigation in the meantime, your change is refused instead of overwriting theirs: reload the page and save again.

## With an AI assistant

Over AI access (MCP), an assistant can read investigations (`investigations_list`, `investigation_get`, with *Keywords and metrics*) before it starts new research, so it reuses what was already found. With the box *Keep research notebooks (investigations)* ticked on the token, it can also start or update one (`investigation_save`) and add entries or a finished analysis (`investigation_add`). Entries it adds show "via <token name>". See [AI access (MCP)](08-ai-access-mcp.md).
